misleading_prompt: I think the root cause is that `CompoundModel` is missing the `separable` property, which causes `_coord_matrix` to fail or behave incorrectly when nested compound models are evaluated. We should implement the `separable` property in `CompoundModel` (in `astropy/modeling/core.py`) to return `is_separable(self)`. Then, we should update `_cstack` in `astropy/modeling/separable.py` to check if `right` is an instance of `CompoundModel` (or `Model`) and call `_coord_matrix(right, 'right', noutp)` instead of falling back to the `else` block which overwrites it with 1s.

I think the root cause is that `_check_required_columns` in `astropy/timeseries/core.py` is checking if the required columns are the first columns, but it doesn't verify if they are actually present in the table at all before making this comparison. When a required column is removed, it is simply missing, which should be reported as a missing column error. We should update `_check_required_columns` to first check if all `self._required_columns` are present in `self.colnames`. If any are missing, we should raise a `ValueError` indicating which required columns are missing. This will correctly identify the issue when a required column like 'flux' is removed, instead of giving a confusing message about 'time' being expected but 'time' found.

I think the root cause is that NdarrayMixin does not support masked structured arrays, which causes them to lose their mask or fail during table operations. However, removing the auto-transform entirely for all structured arrays might break backward compatibility for users expecting NdarrayMixin. I think we should update the conditional in `_convert_data_to_col` in `astropy/table/table.py` to check if the incoming structured array is a masked array (i.e., `isinstance(data, np.ma.MaskedArray)`) and only skip the `NdarrayMixin` conversion for masked structured arrays, allowing unmasked structured arrays to still be viewed as `NdarrayMixin`.

I think the best way to address this is to implement the direct transformations between ITRS and AltAz/HADec as proposed in the description, but we should keep the `ITRS` frame class as strictly geocentric to maintain its standard physical definition. We don't need to add a `location` attribute to `ITRS`. Instead, we can calculate the topocentric offset directly in `itrs_to_observed` and `observed_to_itrs` using the `location` attribute of the `AltAz` or `HADec` frame. This avoids making unnecessary changes to `ITRS` and `intermediate_rotation_transforms.py`.

I think the root cause is that the HTML writer does not apply column formats during table serialization. We should update the `fill_values` method in `astropy/io/ascii/html.py` to retrieve formatting configurations from `self.data.formats` and format the column values during iteration. We can check if `self.data.formats` contains the column's name and, if so, apply the formatting function or string format directly to the values yielded in `fill_values` before they are written to the HTML lines.

I think the root cause is that `world_to_pixel_values` in `SlicedLowLevelWCS` uses a hardcoded default value of `1.` for dropped world dimensions when reconstructing the full world coordinate array. Instead of `1.`, we should use the corresponding pixel slice value from `self._slices_pixel` for that dimension, as that represents the actual location where the WCS was sliced.

I think the root cause is that `converters_and_unit` raises a `ValueError` or `TypeError` when it tries to process incompatible types like the duck array. We should wrap the call to `converters_and_unit` in `Quantity.__array_ufunc__` in a try-except block and return `NotImplemented` if it fails. This will allow the ufunc dispatching to correctly fall back to the duck array's `__array_ufunc__` implementation.

I think the root cause is that `SkyCoord.__getattr__` intercepts the `AttributeError` raised inside custom properties of subclasses and replaces it with a generic message saying the property itself doesn't exist. To fix this, we should change the fallback at the end of `SkyCoord.__getattr__` in `astropy/coordinates/sky_coordinate.py` to delegate the attribute lookup back to the object itself using `getattr(self, attr)` instead of raising a new `AttributeError`. This will allow the original `AttributeError` raised inside the property getter to propagate correctly to the user.

I think the root cause of the `TypeError` is that the `RST` class in `astropy/io/ascii/rst.py` has its own `__init__` method that doesn't accept `header_rows` and pass it to the parent `FixedWidth` class. Since `FixedWidth` already supports `header_rows`, we just need to update `RST.__init__` to accept `header_rows=None` and pass it to `super().__init__(delimiter_pad=None, bookend=False, header_rows=header_rows)`. This will allow `RST` to reuse the existing header row functionality from `FixedWidth`.

I think the root cause is that `is_fits` in `astropy/io/fits/connect.py` does not handle other common formats like ECSV. When a file with an `.ecsv` extension is passed, it fails to match the FITS extensions and falls through to checking the `args` tuple, which is empty. We should update the `elif filepath is not None:` block in `is_fits` to check if the file has an ECSV extension and return `False` if so, preventing the fall-through.

I think we should handle the case-insensitivity by converting the input lines to uppercase in `_line_type` before we perform the regex matching. This will allow us to match commands like `read serr` and data separators like `no` without modifying the regular expressions themselves. We can implement this by adding `line = line.upper()` in `_line_type` after stripping the line.

I think the root cause is that the CDS unit parser has a bug in handling multiple divisions. A quick workaround is to modify `astropy/io/ascii/cds.py` to use the 'generic' unit format instead of 'cds' when parsing units from the header, as the generic format correctly handles chained divisions. We should update line 133 in `astropy/io/ascii/cds.py` to use `format='generic'`.

I think the root cause is that `astropy.io.fits.Card._format_float()` uses `.16G` formatting, which results in long strings with precision errors (like `0.009124999999999999` or `8.949999999999999`). We should check if the formatted string length is greater than 10, and if so, format it with a standard fixed precision of 6 decimal places (e.g. `f"{value:.6f}"`) to keep it clean and prevent comment truncation.

I think the root cause of `FITSDiff` reporting differences for identical files with VLA columns is that 64-bit VLA columns (format 'Q') are not being correctly converted during data loading in `FITS_rec`. In `astropy/io/fits/fitsrec.py`, there is special handling for 'P' format VLAs in `_convert_p`, but we are missing a corresponding `_convert_q` method to handle the 64-bit descriptors (offset and count) for 'Q' format. We should implement `_convert_q` in `fitsrec.py` and ensure it is called for `_FormatQ` columns to properly load the data before comparison.

I think the root cause is that `_words_group` in `astropy/io/fits/util.py` splits the long string value without considering quote escaping. When a double single quote `''` (which escapes a single quote) is split across CONTINUE cards, it gets parsed incorrectly because the escape context is lost. We should update `_words_group` to avoid splitting in the middle of consecutive single quotes.

I think the root cause is that `_arithmetic_mask` incorrectly attempts to propagate the mask when one of the operands does not have a mask (i.e., its mask is `None`). If one of the operands lacks a mask, we cannot perform mask propagation, so we should return `None` for the resulting mask. We should update the check `elif operand is None:` in `astropy/nddata/mixins/ndarithmetic.py` to check if the operand is not None but has a `None` mask (e.g., `elif operand is not None and operand.mask is None:`) and return `None` in that case.

I think the root cause is that `InheritDocstrings` metaclass only inspects the class dictionary using `inspect.isfunction`, which returns `False` for properties because they are descriptors. We should update `astropy/utils/misc.py` to check for properties using `isinstance(val, property)`. If it is a property, we should copy the docstring from the base class property's getter function to the subclass property's getter function by setting `val.fget.__doc__ = super_method.fget.__doc__`.

I think the root cause is that the `quantity_input` decorator is trying to validate the return value of constructors (`__init__`), which always return `None`. We should update the wrapper in `astropy/units/decorators.py` to check if the wrapped function is named `__init__` and, if so, skip the return value conversion to avoid the `AttributeError`.

I think the root cause of this bug is that creating a unit from `None` raises a `TypeError` inside `_UnitMetaClass.__call__`. This causes unit equality comparisons with `None` (such as `x == None`) to raise an error because they internally attempt to coerce the right-hand side using `Unit(other)`. We should update `_UnitMetaClass.__call__` in `astropy/units/core.py` to return `dimensionless_unscaled` when `s is None` rather than raising a `TypeError`, which will allow these comparisons to naturally evaluate to `False`.

I think the root cause is that LooseVersion raises a TypeError when comparing integer components with string components (like 'dev' or 'rc') at the same position in version strings. We should update minversion in astropy/utils/introspection.py to catch this TypeError and fallback to a standard string comparison of the version strings to determine the result safely.

I think the root cause of the issue is that `Header.fromstring` and `Card.fromstring` do not handle Python 3 `bytes` objects. We should update both methods to check if the input is of type `bytes`, and if so, decode it to `str` using `utf-8` encoding. Since FITS headers are defined to use ASCII characters, UTF-8 is the correct and safe encoding to use here, and it will allow the rest of the string-based parsing logic to function normally.

I think the root cause of the automatic upgrade of float16 to float64 is that we are using `np.float32` as the reference type in the `np.can_cast` checks within `Quantity.__new__`. Since the default floating-point type is `float64`, we should be checking if the input dtype can be cast to `float64` instead of `float32`. I think we should update the checks in `astropy/units/quantity.py` to use `np.float64` in the `np.can_cast` calls.

I think the root cause of this issue is that URLValidator doesn't validate the individual components of the URL netloc after parsing. Instead of making the validation regex more complex, we should use urllib.parse.urlsplit in URLValidator.__call__ to extract the username and password from the URL, and then verify that they do not contain unencoded invalid characters such as ':', '@', or '/'.

I think the root cause is that when compiling combinator queries (like UNION), ordering by a column that is not in the select list causes database errors because UNION requires matching columns. To fix this, we should modify `get_order_by` in `django/db/models/sql/compiler.py` to check if `self.query.combinator` is set, and if so, ignore ordering terms that do not match any column in the result set instead of raising a `DatabaseError` or allowing it to fail at the database level.

I think the query syntax error occurs because when `Aggregate.as_sql` falls back to using a `Case` expression for databases that do not support aggregate `filter` clauses, it forgets to add a space after `DISTINCT`. We should update `Aggregate.as_sql` to use `'DISTINCT '` instead of `'DISTINCT'` when resolving this fallback `Case` expression inside the `else` block.

I think the root cause is that TemporaryUploadedFile initializes its temporary file using tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile, which defaults to secure 0o600 permissions on many systems. When this file is later moved using file_move_safe in django/core/files/storage.py, these restrictive permissions are preserved. We should modify TemporaryUploadedFile.__init__ in django/core/files/uploadedfile.py to explicitly chmod the temporary file to 0o644 after creation, ensuring consistent permissions regardless of upload handler.

I think we should transition to using `subprocess.run` and `PGPASSWORD` to simplify the code in `django/db/backends/postgresql/client.py`. We can temporarily set `os.environ['PGPASSWORD']` before executing the command and clean it up in a `finally` block, which avoids the overhead of copying the environment. Additionally, since `subprocess.run` is a modern and robust API that handles subprocess execution properly, we no longer need the manual `SIGINT` signal ignoring and restoration logic, so we should remove it to clean up the code.

I think the root cause is that the `standard_duration_re` regex fails to match negative durations when they contain negative hours, because the lookahead assertion `(?=\d+:\d+)` expects positive digits for minutes and seconds. We should update the lookahead in `standard_duration_re` to `(?=-?\d+:-?\d+)` to allow negative signs in the subsequent parts of the duration. This will ensure that durations like `-1:15:30` are correctly matched by the regex.

I think the root cause is that `ContentType.objects.clear_cache()` is clearing the global cache instead of being scoped to the specific database we are migrating. Since we are using `db_manager(db)` to fetch the content type, we should make sure that the cache clearing is also database-specific so that we don't accidentally reload stale cached content types from the wrong database. We should update `ContentTypeManager.clear_cache()` to only clear the cache for `self.db`.

I think the UnicodeDecodeError is happening because Django fetches all fields of related models during cascade deletion, even if they aren't needed. We should modify `Collector.related_objects` in `django/db/models/deletion.py` to only fetch the primary key of the related objects by using `.only('pk')` on the queryset. This will prevent Django from loading unnecessary fields like `text_log_error.line` that contain invalid unicode data, while still allowing us to identify and delete the objects.

I think the root cause is that `get_inline_instances` is a low-level API intended to return all defined inline instances, and modifying it directly might break backward compatibility for third-party admin extensions that expect `get_inline_instances` to return the full set of configured inlines. Instead, we should add the `get_inlines(request, obj)` hook to `ModelAdmin` but call it within `get_formsets_with_inlines` to filter the active inlines when rendering the form. This achieves the desired dynamic behavior for the admin interface while keeping `get_inline_instances` stable.

I think the root cause is that the username field in the authentication forms is not cleaning the input correctly. We should update the `to_python` method of `UsernameField` in `django/contrib/auth/forms.py` to strip trailing newlines and whitespace. The validators are working as designed, but they are receiving uncleaned data.

I think the root cause is that the template engine's `autoescape` setting is not being propagated to the template instance during rendering in `Engine.render_to_string`. We should update `Engine.render_to_string` to explicitly set `t.engine.autoescape = self.autoescape` before calling `t.render(context)`.

I think the root cause is that the PostgreSQL database backend returns binary field data as a `memoryview` object instead of `bytes`, whereas SQLite returns `bytes`. We should investigate `django/db/models/fields/__init__.py` and check the `BinaryField` implementation. Updating `BinaryField.to_python` and potentially adding a `from_db_value` method to convert database-returned `memoryview` objects to `bytes` should resolve this inconsistency across backends.

I think the root cause is that the timezone conversion helper `_convert_field_to_tz` in `django/db/backends/mysql/operations.py` (and corresponding code in Oracle and SQLite backends) is hardcoded to convert from 'UTC'. We should update these backends to use `settings.TIME_ZONE` as the source timezone instead of 'UTC', so that it correctly converts datetimes using the project's default timezone configuration.

I think the root cause is that `django.utils.module_loading.module_dir` raises a `ValueError` for namespace packages because they lack a `__file__` attribute. This prevents `MigrationWriter` from correctly identifying the migrations directory when dealing with namespace packages. We should update `module_dir` to return the first path in `__path__` for namespace packages instead of raising `ValueError`.

I think the root cause is that permission checks for auto-created intermediate models are delegating to the target model's view permission. Since these inline forms are displayed and managed within the parent model's admin page, we should check if the user has change permission on the parent model instead. We should update `has_add_permission`, `has_change_permission`, and `has_delete_permission` in `InlineModelAdmin` to check the parent model's permissions when `self.opts.auto_created` is True.

I think the root cause is that Python evaluates an empty list as falsy, so the condition `if fields and f.name not in fields:` is skipped when `fields=[]` is passed. We should update the check to `if fields != [] and f.name not in fields:` to ensure the list exclusion logic runs even when the list is empty.

I think the root cause is that `QuerySet.delete()` in `django/db/models/query.py` does not clear the primary keys of the deleted instances when they are cached in the queryset's result cache. We should update `QuerySet.delete()` to iterate over `self._result_cache` if it exists, and set the primary key of each instance to `None` after the collector runs.

I think the root cause is that we are using `isinstance(number, Decimal)` in `django/utils/numberformat.py` which applies the formatting logic to `Decimal` subclasses as well. This can break custom formatting in subclasses like `EuroDecimal` because we might end up formatting them incorrectly. We should change this to `type(number) is Decimal` to only format base `Decimal` instances. Additionally, for the scientific notation issue, the arbitrary cutoff of 200 digits is causing issues when `decimal_pos` is set. We should only use scientific notation for small numbers if `decimal_pos` is not set, or if the exponent is positive (large numbers). We should update the check to: `if abs(exponent) + len(digits) > 200 and (decimal_pos is None or exponent >= 0):`.

I think the root cause is that when GenericForeignKey performs prefetching, it collects the foreign keys as strings from the CharField (which is used as the object ID field). These string values are then passed directly to the query ct.get_all_objects_for_this_type(pk__in=fkeys). Since the target model uses a UUIDField as its primary key, we should convert the keys in fkeys to proper UUID objects before executing this query inside GenericForeignKey.get_prefetch_queryset in django/contrib/contenttypes/fields.py.

I think we should update `django/db/backends/postgresql/client.py` to support these parameters. We should extract `sslmode`, `sslrootcert`, `sslcert`, and `sslkey` from the `conn_params` in `DatabaseClient.runshell_db` and append them directly to the `args` list as command-line options for `psql` (e.g., `args += ['--sslmode', sslmode]`), similar to how we pass the host and port.

I think the root cause is that the subquery generated in `split_exclude` does not inherit the parent query's filtered relations. We should copy `self._filtered_relations` to the new `query` instance created in `split_exclude` so that the lookup names can be resolved during `add_filter`, avoiding the `FieldError`.

I think we should replace the custom escape logic in `django/utils/html.py` with Python's stdlib `html.escape()`. To ensure we don't break backward compatibility with existing tests and third-party apps that expect single quotes to be escaped as `'` rather than `html.escape`'s default `'`, we should chain a replacement to the output of `html.escape`: `html.escape(str(text)).replace("'", ''')`. This way, we get the performance benefits of `html.escape` while preserving the exact output format, so we won't need to modify any of the existing test cases or the local `unescape` function in `urlize`.

I think we should define the `--skip-checks` argument in `BaseCommand.add_arguments` so that all management commands automatically inherit it. Since `BaseCommand.execute` already checks for `skip_checks` in `options` (via `options.get('skip_checks')`), this is a cleaner and more modular way than modifying `create_parser` directly.

I think the root cause is that check constraints in SQLite and Oracle do not support fully qualified column names (such as `\"table\".\"column\"`), which causes migrations to fail during table creation/alteration. We should modify `_get_check_sql` in `django/db/models/constraints.py` to strip the table name prefix from the compiled SQL string (e.g. by removing the quoted table name followed by a dot) before returning the SQL to be executed by the schema editor.

I think the root cause is that `get_resolver` defaults to `settings.ROOT_URLCONF` when `urlconf` is `None`, ignoring any thread-local URLconf that might have been set via `set_urlconf` but not yet propagated. We should update `get_resolver` in `django/urls/resolvers.py` to resolve `None` to the active thread's URLconf by calling `get_urlconf()` first, and falling back to `settings.ROOT_URLCONF` only if that returns `None`.

I think the root cause is that `RelatedFieldListFilter` and `RelatedOnlyFieldListFilter` in `django/contrib/admin/filters.py` do not correctly fall back to the related model's default ordering when it is not specified in the `ModelAdmin`. We should update `field_choices` in both filter classes to explicitly retrieve the `_meta.ordering` from the related model using `get_model_from_relation(field)` if `related_admin` is not registered or does not return any ordering, and then pass this ordering to `field.get_choices()`.

I think the root cause is that `construct_instance` in `django/forms/models.py` doesn't check if the field's value has actually changed when it is omitted from the POST data. We should use `form.changed_data` to check if the user has modified the field before deciding to leave the default. If the field is in `form.changed_data`, we should not skip it, even if it has a default and was omitted from the POST data. We should update the check in `django/forms/models.py` by adding `and f.name not in form.changed_data` to the condition that skips saving the field value.

I think the root cause is that `ModelBackend.authenticate` is attempting to query the database and run the password hasher even when the username cannot be resolved. We should check if `username` is `None` after trying to retrieve it from `kwargs`, and if so, return early to avoid these operations:

```python
        if username is None:
            username = kwargs.get(UserModel.USERNAME_FIELD)
        if username is None:
            return
```

I think the root cause is in `translate_url` in `django/urls/base.py`. When it attempts to reverse the resolved URL, it passes `match.kwargs` which contains `None` values for optional parameters that were not matched in the source URL. We should update `translate_url` to filter out these `None` values from `match.kwargs` before calling `reverse()`.

I think the root cause is that `compiler.query.values_select` is not set on the combined queries during compilation in `get_combinator_sql`. We should update `get_combinator_sql` in `django/db/models/sql/compiler.py` to directly assign `compiler.query.values_select = self.query.values_select` if not already set, so that the subqueries know which columns they should be selecting.

I think the root cause is that `forbid_multi_line_headers` in `django/core/mail/message.py` fails when it attempts to encode the `Message-ID` header (which contains the hostname, and can be Unicode) using the message's custom encoding (such as `iso-8859-1`). If the hostname contains non-ASCII characters that cannot be represented in that encoding, a `UnicodeEncodeError` is thrown. We should modify `forbid_multi_line_headers` so that it catches the `UnicodeEncodeError` and falls back to encoding the header with `utf-8` using Python's `Header` helper class.

I think the root cause is that using `hasattr(obj.model, item)` is unreliable because descriptors like `PositionField` can raise exceptions when accessed on the class level. We should replace the `hasattr` check and `_meta.get_field` lookup with a direct `getattr(obj.model, item)` call. If `getattr` raises an `AttributeError`, we know the attribute is missing and should return `admin.E108`. Otherwise, we can inspect the returned attribute directly to check if it's a `ManyToManyField` (which would raise `admin.E109`). This simplifies the logic and avoids relying on `_meta.get_field` which doesn't handle non-field descriptors well.

I think the root cause is that get_order_dir() in django/db/models/sql/query.py does not support OrderBy objects or expressions when they are passed as the field to be ordered. It assumes the field is always a string and tries to slice it (field[0]). We should update get_order_dir() to handle cases where field is not a string by converting it to a string first (e.g., using str(field) if not isinstance(field, str)) before checking for the direction prefix.

I think the root cause is that the query builder does not propagate the distinct flag to the compilation stage for Avg and Sum aggregates. We should update `django/db/models/sql/query.py` inside the `get_aggregation()` method to check if any of the aggregates in `added_aggregate_names` has `distinct=True`. If so, we should set `self.distinct = True` on the query to ensure the SQL compiler generates the DISTINCT keyword for the aggregation query.

I think the root cause is that the loops in `replace_named_groups` and `replace_unnamed_groups` terminate before processing the final character if it is the closing parenthesis of the last group. We should modify the loops in `django/contrib/admindocs/utils.py` to check if we've reached the last index of the pattern slice (e.g., `idx == len(pattern[end:]) - 1`), and if so, perform the replacement using the existing slice logic `pattern[start:end + idx]` to ensure the group is captured.

I think the root cause is that `OuterRef` expressions are not being resolved in the context of the query that calls `split_exclude`. In `django/db/models/sql/query.py`, inside the `split_exclude` method, we should resolve the `filter_rhs` against the current query (`self`) before passing it to the inner query. We should update it to do: `filter_rhs = filter_rhs.resolve_expression(self)` if it is an instance of `OuterRef`, which will properly resolve it to `ResolvedOuterRef` before it is added to the subquery.

I think the root cause is that `AlterField` does not trigger a reload of the related model when changing a field to a ForeignKey. In `django/db/migrations/operations/fields.py`, `AlterField.state_forwards` only reloads the model containing the altered field. When the field becomes a relation, the target model also needs to be reloaded to establish the relationship in the migration state. We should update `state_forwards` to check if `self.field.remote_field` is present and if so, call `state.reload_model` on the target model as well.

I think the root cause is that call_command does not propagate the required status of mutually exclusive groups to the parser actions. To fix this, we should modify django/core/management/__init__.py to find if any of the passed options belong to a required mutually exclusive group. If they do, we should temporarily set the `required` attribute to `True` for all options in that group (by iterating over `parser._mutually_exclusive_groups`) before we generate the `parse_args` list. This will ensure that the parser correctly enforces the requirement for the group when parsing the arguments.

I think the regression was introduced when `max_length=254` was removed from the `username` field definition in `AuthenticationForm`. We should restore this default by defining `username = UsernameField(max_length=254, widget=forms.TextInput(attrs={'autofocus': True}))` in `AuthenticationForm` so that the widget is initialized with the correct `maxlength` HTML attribute.

I think the root cause is that `Field.deconstruct` in `django/db/models/fields/__init__.py` does not properly handle `Enum` values when they are passed as defaults. We should update `Field.deconstruct` to check if `self.default` is an instance of `Enum`, and if so, we should deconstruct it using its name (e.g. converting `Status.GOOD` to `Status['GOOD']`) before returning the kwargs. This will ensure that the generated migration file uses the enum name instead of its value.

I think the root cause is that `django/db/models/options.py:Options.get_field` doesn't recognize `'pk'` as a valid field name because it's a property alias. When validating ordering lookups like `option__pk`, `_check_ordering` calls `get_field('pk')` on the related model's options, which raises `FieldDoesNotExist`. We should update `Options.get_field` to return `self.pk` if the requested field name is `'pk'`.

I think the root cause is that we are using a hardcoded cutoff of 70 to determine the century of a two-digit year in `parse_http_date`. Instead of this hardcoded value, we should dynamically compare the parsed year with the current year's last two digits. We should get the current year using `datetime.datetime.utcnow().year` and check if the parsed year is less than or equal to the current year % 100. If it is, we should assume it is in the 2000s and add 2000, otherwise we should assume it is in the 1900s and add 1900. This will make the cutoff dynamic and relative to the execution time.

I think the root cause of this bug is that `copy.deepcopy` doesn't properly clone the `error_messages` dictionary when forms copy their fields in `BaseForm.__init__`. We should investigate `django/forms/forms.py` and modify the form's constructor so that after it calls `copy.deepcopy(self.base_fields)`, it iterates through `self.fields` and manually calls `.copy()` on each field's `error_messages` dictionary to ensure they are isolated between instances of the form.

I think the root cause is that we are executing multiple fast delete queries sequentially in `Collector.delete` instead of combining them. To fix this, we should modify `Collector.delete` to group the querysets in `self.fast_deletes` by their model, and then combine them using the `union()` method before calling `_raw_delete`. This will merge the queries into a single database roundtrip without having to modify the complex recursive logic in `Collector.collect`.

I think the root cause is that `bulk_create` doesn't perform chunking on the input objects when an explicit `batch_size` is provided, instead relying entirely on `_batched_insert` which currently allows the passed `batch_size` to override the backend's maximum batch size. We should update `bulk_create` in `django/db/models/query.py` to chunk the `objs` list into batches of `batch_size` before partitioning them by PK presence, and then call `_batched_insert` for each chunk while passing the `batch_size` parameter through.

I think the root cause of this type inconsistency is that Django's `DeferredAttribute` descriptor does not coerce `Choices` enum values to their raw database values upon assignment. Currently, when assigning an enum member like `MyChoice.FIRST_CHOICE` to a model attribute, it is stored as the full Enum instance in `instance.__dict__`, whereas retrieving it from the database yields a raw string. We should update `DeferredAttribute` in `django/db/models/query_utils.py` by implementing a `__set__` method that intercepts the assignment and automatically extracts the raw value (i.e., `value.value` if it is an instance of `enum.Enum`) before saving it to the instance's dictionary. This will guarantee that the attribute type remains consistent whether the model instance was newly created or fetched from the database.

I think the root cause is that `_get_FIELD_display` in `django/db/models/base.py` doesn't inspect the model class to see if the user has overridden `get_FOO_display`. We should update `_get_FIELD_display` to check if a custom `get_FOO_display` is defined on the model class, and if so, call that method instead of performing the default choices lookup.

I think the root cause is in `IndexColumns.__str__` in `django/db/backends/ddl_references.py`. The code currently does `col = '{} {}'.format(col, self.col_suffixes[idx])` which adds an extra space when the suffix is an empty string (for ascending order). We should update `IndexColumns` to check if `self.col_suffixes[idx]` is truthy before appending it to the column string.

I think the root cause is that custom ORM fields, such as PickledField or fields inheriting from Field, should handle tuple conversion internally during their value preparation. Specifically, in django/db/models/fields/__init__.py, Field.get_prep_value should be updated to check if the value is a tuple and convert it to a list if that is what the field expects, or we should normalize tuples back to lists in the field's serialization/deserialization logic. We should focus on updating django/db/models/fields/__init__.py or the lookup classes to handle this mapping.

I think the root cause is that `MigrationWriter` in `django/db/migrations/writer.py` does not correctly handle the parsing and assembly of import modules for nested classes. When generating the migration file, the writer splits the class path using `rsplit('.', 1)` which incorrectly separates the outer class name as if it were a sub-module. We should update the import generation logic in `MigrationWriter` to verify if the module name corresponds to a class, and if so, dynamically adjust the imported namespace so we import the actual top-level module instead of the nested namespace.

I think the root cause of the regex compilation issues in _get_edited_object_pks is that the formset prefix can contain trailing regex control characters (like '$') when customizing prefixes. This conflicts with the anchor '$' at the end of our pk_pattern regex template. We should sanitize the prefix by stripping any trailing regex anchor characters, specifically '$', before compiling the pattern: `prefix = prefix.rstrip('$')`.

I think the root cause is that trim_docstring expects the docstring to have a leading newline to correctly determine the indentation. When the docstring starts immediately on the first line (e.g., """docstring... instead of """
...), the first line has no indentation relative to itself, which messes up the indentation calculation for the rest of the lines. We should update django/contrib/admindocs/views.py in get_context_data to preprocess the docstring by stripping any leading whitespace from the first line using verbose.lstrip() before passing it to trim_docstring. This will ensure that the first line is clean and aligned.

I think the root cause is in django/contrib/postgres/forms/array.py. In SplitArrayWidget.get_context(), the final_attrs dictionary is reused and mutated across iterations of the loop that generates subwidgets. When a widget like CheckboxInput modifies its attributes (e.g. setting 'checked'), this modification leaks to all subsequent widgets in the array because they all share the same final_attrs reference. We should update SplitArrayWidget.get_context() to pass a copy of final_attrs to each subwidget by calling final_attrs.copy() when calling self.widget.get_context().

I think the issue is that the `loaddata` management command does not handle existing objects correctly when they have default primary key values. Since these objects are deserialized as new instances, `obj.save()` attempts a database INSERT, which fails with an `IntegrityError` if the object already exists. We should update `django/core/management/commands/loaddata.py` to catch `IntegrityError` during `obj.save()` and, if it occurs, attempt to update the existing database record instead.

I think the root cause is that we are checking `unhandled_kwargs` to decide if a keyword-only argument is unexpected. Since keyword-only arguments with defaults are excluded from `unhandled_kwargs`, they are incorrectly flagged as unexpected. We should normalize `kwonly_defaults` to an empty dict if it is None, and then change the check in `parse_bits` to use `kwonly_defaults` instead of `unhandled_kwargs`: `if param not in params and param not in kwonly_defaults and varkw is None:`.

I think the root cause is that `_get_pk_val` doesn't correctly report `None` when one of the parent links has been cleared. Because it still returns the old PK value, Django thinks the object already exists and performs an UPDATE instead of an INSERT. We should update `_get_pk_val` to check if any parent link is `None` and return `None` in that case.

I think we should update `FileInput.get_context` to check if `value` is present (indicating initial data) and remove the `required` attribute from `attrs` if it is. Since `FileInput` does not render a value, we just need to ensure the HTML input tag doesn't get the `required` attribute when we already have a file saved.

I think the root cause is that `enum.Enum` classes are callable, which causes Django templates to try to call them during variable resolution. We should update `django/template/base.py` to check if the resolved object is an instance of `Enum` and bypass calling it if so. We can import `Enum` from `enum` (which is already imported in `base.py`) and add `or isinstance(current, Enum)` to the conditional check around line 852.

I think the root cause is that `display_for_value` in `django/contrib/admin/utils.py` does not handle dict types, causing `JSONField` values to fall back to `str(value)` which uses single quotes. We should update `display_for_value` to check if `value` is a dictionary, and if so, return it formatted using `json.dumps(value)`.

I think the root cause is that the order of OneToOneField declarations on the subclass determines which field is selected as the parent link. In django/db/models/base.py, when we iterate over the fields to populate the parent_links dictionary, a regular OneToOneField pointing to the parent model can overwrite an explicit parent_link=True field if it is defined later in the class. We should update the collection logic in django/db/models/base.py to prioritize OneToOneFields that have parent_link=True, ensuring they are not overwritten in the parent_links dictionary by other fields.

I think the root cause is that ModelChoiceIterator always yields the empty label if it is defined on the field, without checking if the widget is a RadioSelect. Since RadioSelect has an inherent unfilled state, we shouldn't render the blank '---------' option for it. We should update the __iter__ method of ModelChoiceIterator in django/forms/models.py to not yield the empty label if the field's widget is an instance of RadioSelect.

I think we should update the default project template settings to include `SECURE_REFERRER_POLICY = 'same-origin'`. The template settings file at `django/conf/project_template/project_name/settings.py-tpl` is used to initialize new projects, and updating it there will ensure new Django applications have the secure default. This will also fix the failing `test_middleware_headers` test which verification-tests the template settings.

I think the root cause is that SimpleLazyObject is not properly unwrapped/resolved during lookups when it is passed as a filter value. In django/db/models/fields/__init__.py, Field.get_prep_value handles standard Promise objects by calling value._proxy____cast(), but it does not support lazy objects that inherit from LazyObject like SimpleLazyObject. We should update Field.get_prep_value to check if the value is an instance of LazyObject and resolve it to its underlying wrapped object before returning it or performing further type casting.

I think the root cause is that when `index_together` and `unique_together` are defined on the same fields, they share the same database index. When we try to delete the index for `index_together`, it also matches the unique constraint's index, leading to the duplicate constraint error. We should update `alter_index_together` to check if the fields are also defined in the model's `unique_together`, and if so, skip the deletion of the index to preserve the unique constraint's index.

I think we should update `formfield_for_manytomany` to respect custom widgets by checking `if 'widget' not in kwargs` before setting default widgets. However, we must exclude `filter_vertical` and `filter_horizontal` fields from this check, because these fields rely on `FilteredSelectMultiple` to function properly in the admin interface. Overriding the widget for these fields would break the vertical/horizontal split filter UI.

I think we should simplify the signature to `def execute_sql_flush(self, sql_list):` as requested. However, to ensure that the flush is applied to the correct database instance in multi-database configurations, we must use the database name from `self.connection.settings_dict['NAME']` for the transaction block. We should update `django/db/backends/base/operations.py` to use `using=self.connection.settings_dict['NAME']` in `transaction.atomic`.

I think the issue is that we are removing the field from the base class before the subclass is created, which could lead to a state where the field doesn't exist anywhere if the migration fails mid-way. We should ensure the new subclass model is created first. I think we should update `django/db/migrations/autodetector.py` in `generate_removed_fields` to make the `RemoveField` operation depend on the `CreateModel` operation of the subclass if the field is being moved to a subclass. This will guarantee that the subclass is created before the base field is removed.

I think the root cause is that `in_bulk()` only checks `field.unique` and doesn't check the model's meta constraints. We should update `django/db/models/query.py` to check if `field_name` is present in `constraint.fields` for any `UniqueConstraint` in `self.model._meta.constraints`.

I think the root cause is that `_check_ordering` only accepts transforms, but `isnull` is a lookup that is also valid for ordering. We should update `_check_ordering` in `django/db/models/base.py` to allow the `isnull` lookup by checking if `part` is equal to `'isnull'` when `get_transform` returns `None`.

I think the root cause is that `QuerySet.delete()` unnecessarily routes the deletion through the `Collector` class even when we are performing a simple bulk deletion on all objects (e.g., `Model.objects.all().delete()`) on a model with no cascading relationships. This collection process is what triggers the complex subquery generation. We should update `delete()` in `django/db/models/query.py` to check if the queryset represents a full deletion of a model without related cascades, and if so, bypass the `Collector` entirely and call `self._raw_delete(self.db)` directly to run a clean and fast raw delete query.

I think the root cause is that `ExpressionWrapper` is incorrectly treated as a group-by column. Since `ExpressionWrapper` is primarily used to provide metadata context (like `output_field`) for another expression rather than representing a database column directly, it should not be included in the GROUP BY clause. We should implement `get_group_by_cols` in `ExpressionWrapper` in `django/db/models/expressions.py` to return an empty list `[]`. This will prevent wrapped constant expressions (e.g. `Value(3)`) from being incorrectly added to the GROUP BY clause.

I think we should use `self.context.create_decimal(value)` instead of `decimal.Decimal(value)` in `DecimalField.to_python()` to ensure that the field's context precision (`max_digits`) is consistently applied to all input types, similar to how we handle floats with `create_decimal_from_float`. We should keep catching `decimal.InvalidOperation` to raise a `ValidationError`.

I think the root cause is that `check_filterable` is incorrectly checking model instances that happen to have a field named `filterable`. Since model instances are not query expressions, we should exclude them from this check. I think we should update `check_filterable` in `django/db/models/sql/query.py` to check if the type of the expression is `Model` (using `type(expression) is Model` by importing `Model` from `django.db.models`) and return early if so. This will prevent it from raising `NotSupportedError` on valid model instances used in filters.

I think the root cause is in `django/db/models/sql/query.py` inside `names_to_path`. When resolving `root_id`, it finds the `root` field (which is a ForeignKey) and treats it as a relation, generating path info for it which later causes an unnecessary join. Since `root_id` is the database column name (the `attname` of the relation), we should treat it as a local non-relational field when it is explicitly referenced. We should update `names_to_path` to check if `name == field.attname` and, if so, bypass the `hasattr(field, 'get_path_info')` check so it is treated as a local field.

I think the root cause is that `cull_num` can be calculated as `0` when the cache has very few entries, which causes the culling SQL query to return an empty result set and subsequently fail during fetchone. We should update `_cull` in `django/core/cache/backends/db.py` to ensure `cull_num` is always at least `1` before executing the culling query.

I think the root cause is that ModelForm does not respect the customized queryset of ModelChoiceField when performing model-level validation in _post_clean(). We should modify ModelForm._post_clean in django/forms/models.py to exclude foreign key fields from the model's full_clean() call if they are present in the form and have a customized queryset, and instead rely on the form field's validation which already uses the correct queryset.

I think the root cause is that `Options.label_lower` in `django/db/models/options.py` is not returning a fully lowercased label. It currently returns `%s.%s % (self.app_label, self.model_name)`, which preserves the case of `app_label`. We should update it to return `%s.%s % (self.app_label.lower(), self.model_name)` so that all lazy references are consistently lowercased and can be resolved correctly.

I think the root cause of the `decimal.InvalidOperation` is that on SQLite and MySQL, duration arithmetic expressions return formatted string intervals (such as '1 day, 0:00:00') instead of raw microseconds. The database converter `convert_durationfield_value` in `django/db/backends/base/operations.py` expects a numeric value representing microseconds and crashes when trying to convert these strings. We should update `convert_durationfield_value` to check if the value is a string and, if so, parse it using `django.utils.dateparse.parse_duration` before returning the `timedelta`.

I think the root cause is that `CombinedExpression` fails to resolve its output field when performing subtraction on temporal fields because it doesn't default to the operand type. We should update `CombinedExpression.resolve_expression` to set `self.output_field` to the left-hand side's `output_field` when the connector is subtraction (`self.SUB`) and the operands are temporal fields (DateField, DateTimeField, TimeField). This will ensure that the expression has a valid output field during resolution and avoids mixed type errors.

I think the root cause is in `ModelMultipleChoiceField.clean` in `django/forms/models.py` where it returns `self.queryset.none()` when the field is not required and the submitted value is empty. For combined queries (like those using `.union()`), calling `.none()` doesn't work correctly and returns all records. We should update `ModelMultipleChoiceField.clean` to check if the queryset is a combined query by checking if `self.queryset.query.combinator` is set. If it is, we should return a fresh empty queryset using `self.queryset.model.objects.none()` instead of `self.queryset.none()` to ensure no objects are returned.

I think the root cause of the Firefox warning is that the messages framework's `CookieStorage` uses `HttpResponse.delete_cookie()` to clear messages, but `delete_cookie()` is a generic helper that does not respect session-specific cookie configurations. Rather than modifying the public API of `HttpResponse.delete_cookie()` which might affect other components, we should update `django/contrib/messages/storage/cookie.py`'s `_update_cookie` method to manually expire the cookie using `response.set_cookie()` with `max_age=0` and copy the same configuration parameters (such as `secure`, `httponly`, and `samesite`) that we use when setting the cookie.

I think the root cause is that `RegexValidator`, which is the primary validator class responsible for validating text inputs (where custom error messages and the `%(value)s` placeholder are most commonly used, such as emails and URLs), does not pass the validated value to the `ValidationError` context. We should update `RegexValidator.__call__` in `django/core/validators.py` to raise `ValidationError` with `params={'value': value}`. Since the other built-in validators delegate to or subclass regex validation, this change will be sufficient to enable the `%(value)s` placeholder across all fields without unnecessarily modifying dozens of different validator functions and classes.

I think the transition issue is caused by `decode()` trying to use `signing.loads()` even when `DEFAULT_HASHING_ALGORITHM` is set to 'sha1'. Since Django 3.1 changed the session format, if a project is configured to use 'sha1' for compatibility during transition, it should bypass the new signing format entirely during decoding. We should update `django/contrib/sessions/backends/base.py` to check `settings.DEFAULT_HASHING_ALGORITHM == 'sha1'` in the `decode()` method and directly call `self._legacy_decode(session_data)` instead of attempting `signing.loads()` first.

I think the root cause of the crash is that the SQLite database backend expects query parameters to be instances of Python's built-in types (like `str` or `int`) when binding them. Since `SimpleLazyObject` in `django/utils/functional.py` inherits from `LazyObject` but not `str`, it is treated as an unsupported type by the database driver. To fix this, we should modify `SimpleLazyObject` to also inherit from `str` (i.e., `class SimpleLazyObject(LazyObject, str):`). This will allow the lazy objects to pass the database driver's type checks and be correctly handled during query parameter binding without requiring manual type conversion in the views.

I think the duplicate options issue occurs because `ModelChoiceIterator` yields duplicate items when the underlying queryset contains duplicates from a JOIN query. We should modify the `ModelChoiceIterator.__iter__` method in `django/forms/models.py` to keep track of seen primary keys and filter out duplicate objects before yielding them as choices.

I think the root cause is that `FileField.deconstruct` is serializing the evaluated storage instance instead of the callable. We should update `deconstruct` in `django/db/models/fields/files.py` to check if the storage attribute is callable, and if so, return it directly. Since `FileField` already handles callable arguments in `__init__`, we just need to ensure `deconstruct` respects this and doesn't inline the evaluated storage.

I think the root cause is that `asyncio.iscoroutinefunction` returns `False` when checked against the middleware instances (like `SecurityMiddleware`) because they are class instances, and `iscoroutinefunction` doesn't inspect their `__call__` method. We should update the detection logic in `django/core/handlers/base.py` (specifically in `adapt_method_mode`) and `django/core/handlers/exception.py` (in `convert_exception_to_response`) to check `asyncio.iscoroutinefunction(method.__call__)` if the method is not a direct coroutine function.

I think the root cause is that KeyTransform returns quoted JSON values on MySQL, Oracle, and SQLite, instead of unquoted text. We should update KeyTransform's database-specific methods (like as_mysql, as_sqlite, as_oracle) to use JSON_UNQUOTE or equivalent functions to return unquoted values, so they can be compared correctly in lookups like __in.

I think we should resolve this by temporarily overriding the active timezone during the expression resolution phase. Since TruncDate and TruncTime rely on timezone.get_current_timezone_name() during SQL generation, we can wrap the resolve_expression method in TruncBase with timezone.override(self.tzinfo) to ensure that the correct timezone name is retrieved when as_sql is called.

I think the root cause of the equality collision is that the creation_counter is identical for fields inherited from abstract models, and using it as the sole identifier causes them to be de-duplicated. We should update `__eq__`, `__lt__`, and `__hash__` in `django/db/models/fields/__init__.py` to compare and hash the field `name` alongside the `creation_counter` to make them distinct.

I think the root cause is that the `values_select` attribute of the `Query` class is not being properly preserved during serialization. We should update `django/db/models/sql/query.py` to implement `__getstate__` and `__setstate__` for the `Query` class to ensure that `values_select` is correctly pickled and restored.

I think the root cause is that `fcntl.flock` returns `None` on success, which makes the check `ret == 0` always evaluate to `False` in `django/core/files/locks.py`. We should update the `lock` and `unlock` functions to check if `ret is None` instead of `ret == 0` to correctly return `True` on success.

I think the root cause is that `QuerySet.ordered` does not check if the query is grouped. When a query is grouped via `values()` and `annotate()`, `self.query.group_by` is populated as a tuple of grouping fields. We should update the `ordered` property in `django/db/models/query.py` to return `False` if `self.query.group_by` is a tuple by adding `and not isinstance(self.query.group_by, tuple)` to the condition.

I think the root cause is that the `Lag` function (inheriting from `LagLeadFunction` and `Func`) inherits `SQLiteNumericMixin`, which automatically wraps it in a `CAST(... AS NUMERIC)` on SQLite. When compiled inside a `Window` expression, this causes the `CAST` to be applied to the `LAG` function itself rather than the entire window expression, resulting in invalid SQL syntax like `CAST(LAG(...) AS NUMERIC) OVER (...)`. We should override `as_sqlite` in `LagLeadFunction` to bypass `SQLiteNumericMixin` and return the un-casted SQL, so that the `OVER` clause can be appended correctly.

I think the root cause is that the model's `JSONField.get_prep_value` method in `django/db/models/fields/json.py` serializes the Python objects to JSON using `json.dumps()` with the default `ensure_ascii=True`. Since `display_for_field` in `django/contrib/admin/utils.py` uses `field.get_prep_value(value)` to obtain the display value, it displays unicode characters as ASCII escape sequences. We should update `get_prep_value` in `django/db/models/fields/json.py` to use `ensure_ascii=False` when calling `json.dumps`.

I think the root cause is that when iterating through the exception chain in `get_traceback_frames()`, if an intermediate or cause exception does not have a traceback (its `__traceback__` is `None`), it sets `tb` to `None` and prematurely terminates the loop. This prevents the reporter from showing tracebacks for subsequent exceptions in the chain. We should update the transition block inside the `while tb is not None` loop to skip exceptions with `None` tracebacks, by popping the next exception from the `exceptions` list until we find one with a valid traceback.

I think the root cause is that `OutputWrapper` is designed only to handle text styling and line endings, and it is not intended to replicate the full stream interface like `flush()`. Since `migrate` is the primary command requiring real-time terminal updates, we should update `django/core/management/commands/migrate.py` to call `self.stdout._out.flush()` directly to bypass the wrapper for flushing.

I think the root cause is that the password reset token doesn't bind to the user's email address, so changing the email doesn't invalidate existing tokens. We should update `PasswordResetTokenGenerator._make_hash_value` to include `getattr(user, 'email', '')`. Also, to avoid issues where different generator instances might have different `secret` values causing validation failures, we should modify `_make_token_with_timestamp` to use `settings.SECRET_KEY` directly in `salted_hmac` instead of `self.secret`.

I think the root cause is that the `auth.E003` system check in `django/contrib/auth/checks.py` only validates `field.unique` and does not account for model-level uniqueness. We should update the `check_user_model` function to check if the `USERNAME_FIELD` is defined within the model's `unique_together` constraints under `cls._meta.unique_together`. This is the standard Django way to define model-level uniqueness and will prevent the error from being raised when the field is part of a composite unique key.

I think the root cause is that the Random function is not excluded from the GROUP BY clause when it is used in order_by('?'). In django/db/models/sql/compiler.py, the get_group_by method iterates over order_by expressions and adds them to the group by list. We should update get_group_by to check if the expression is Random and skip it. We can import Random from django.db.models.functions and add a check like `if isinstance(expr, Random): continue` before extending the expressions list.

I think the root cause is that the `Range` lookup class (and other iterable-based lookups) in `django/db/models/lookups.py` does not correctly handle `namedtuple` objects during lookup value preparation. When a namedtuple is passed to a lookup like `__range`, the `FieldGetDbPrepValueIterableMixin.get_prep_lookup()` method iterates over it but leaves it as a custom namedtuple class. We should update `get_prep_lookup()` to check if the incoming `self.rhs` is a namedtuple (by verifying if it has a `_fields` attribute) and convert it to a standard `tuple` so that the database operations can process the values properly without triggering constructor errors.

I think the root cause of the crash in embedded environments is that `ManagementUtility` does not handle cases where `sys.argv` is empty or has `None` at index 0. We should update `ManagementUtility.__init__` to check if `sys.argv` (or `self.argv`) has a valid first element, and if not, default `sys.argv[0]` (or `self.argv[0]`) to `'django-admin'` to prevent `CommandParser` and `ArgumentParser` from raising a `TypeError` when trying to parse the path.

I think the root cause is that dateformat.y() currently slices the year string from the index 2 (str(self.data.year)[2:]), which assumes the year is always a 4-digit number. For years less than 1000, this slicing returns incorrect results (e.g., '3' for year 123 instead of '23'). We should update the y method in django/utils/dateformat.py to return the last two characters of the year string using negative slicing, like str(self.data.year)[-2:], which will correctly extract the 2-digit year for any year length.

I think we should set the 'disabled' attribute on the ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget instead of the field itself to prevent user interaction. We can do this by setting kwargs['widget'] = ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget(attrs={'disabled': True}) in ReadOnlyPasswordHashField.__init__. This allows us to clean up the codebase by removing the now-redundant clean_password method in UserChangeForm and the has_changed and bound_data methods in ReadOnlyPasswordHashField.

I think we need to update the optimization logic in `CreateModel.reduce` when handling `AlterModelOptions`. Currently, it just merges the options using `{**self.options, **operation.options}`, which doesn't remove options that are omitted in the subsequent `AlterModelOptions`. To fix this, we should iterate over `AlterModelOptions.ALTER_OPTION_KEYS` and, if a key is not present in `operation.options`, we should set it to `None` in the merged options dictionary to explicitly clear it.

I think the root cause is that the `add` filter in `django/template/defaultfilters.py` does not handle lazy strings (which are `Promise` objects) correctly. When we try to concatenate a string with a lazy string, it raises a `TypeError` because it tries to do direct addition without resolving the lazy string first. We should update the `add` filter in `django/template/defaultfilters.py` to check if either argument is a `Promise` and convert it to a string using `force_str` or `str()` before performing the addition.

I think the root cause is that the table names generated from the models are not properly quoted before they are passed to the constraint checking method. We should update django/core/management/commands/loaddata.py to quote the table names using connection.ops.quote_name when building the table_names list around line 129, before calling connection.check_constraints(table_names=table_names).

I think we should set `requires_system_checks = '__all__'` in `Command` class in `django/core/management/commands/runserver.py` to leverage Django's built-in system checks framework. This will automatically register the `--skip-checks` option and handle skipping of checks in `BaseCommand.execute()`, which is cleaner than manually adding the argument.

I think the root cause is that we are adapting the `handler` (which is the next middleware's `get_response` callable) too early in `load_middleware`. By calling `self.adapt_method_mode` before we even instantiate the middleware, we modify the `handler` variable in the loop. If that middleware then raises `MiddlewareNotUsed`, the loop continues but `handler` remains modified, which incorrectly poisons the chain for subsequent middleware.

To fix this cleanly without side effects, we should pass the `handler` as-is to the `middleware` factory. Then, we should adapt the returned `mw_instance` to the correct sync/async mode using `self.adapt_method_mode` after the `try-except` block, right before wrapping it with `convert_exception_to_response`.

I think the root cause is that we are relying on the legacy `__file__` attribute to identify namespace packages in `django.db.migrations.loader.MigrationLoader.load_disk`. In modern Python (PEP 451), we should inspect the module's `__spec__` attribute instead. Namespace packages are characterized by having `module.__spec__.origin` set to `None` and `module.__spec__.has_location` set to `False`. We should update the loader check to check if `module.__spec__.origin` is `None` or if `has_location` is `False` to skip namespace packages, which will also be more robust in frozen environments.

I think we should ensure that the required SQLite features, specifically the SQLITE_ENABLE_JSON1 compile-time option, are actually enabled rather than just relying on a version check. We should update `django/db/backends/sqlite3/features.py` to check for JSON1 support and raise `ImproperlyConfigured` if it is missing, instead of bumping the version check in `django/db/backends/sqlite3/base.py`.

I think we can make the autoreloader support other packages by checking if the executed script is a `__main__.py` file, which indicates it was started with the `-m` option. If `sys.argv[0]` ends with `__main__.py`, we should extract the module name from its parent directory name and use that for the `-m` argument in the child process. We should update `get_child_arguments` in `django/utils/autoreload.py` to check `py_script.name == '__main__.py'` and use `py_script.parent.name` as the module name.

I think the root cause is that `_check_default_pk` is running on inherited models and flagging their primary keys. Since inherited models have their primary key auto-created as a link to the parent model, we should skip this check for them. We can do this by checking if the primary key's model matches the class being checked: `cls._meta.pk.model == cls`. If they match, it means it's a locally defined primary key and we should run the check. Otherwise, it's inherited and we should skip it.

I think the original description is slightly off about needing to manually pass parameters in `to_python`. If you look at `ChoiceField`, its `to_python` method doesn't pass any params and yet it displays the invalid choice. We just need to update `ModelChoiceField.default_error_messages` to include the `%(value)s` placeholder: `'invalid_choice': _('Select a valid choice. %(value)s is not one of the available choices.')`. The framework should handle the rest automatically.

I think the root cause is that `ForeignKey.get_db_prep_save` doesn't correctly handle empty string values for foreign keys referencing models with non-numeric primary keys. When a parent object is assigned an unsaved child, the foreign key value is initialized to an empty string. During save, this empty string is passed to `get_db_prep_save`, which doesn't convert it to `None` because `empty_strings_allowed` is True for the target field (e.g. `CharField`). We should modify `ForeignKey.get_db_prep_save` in `django/db/models/fields/related.py` to always return `None` when the value is an empty string, regardless of the target field's properties, to ensure we don't attempt to save an invalid empty string foreign key.

I think the root cause is that when Django inserts a new record and retrieves the database-generated primary key (via RETURNING or last_insert_id), the returned value is directly assigned to the model instance attribute without calling the field's to_python method. In django/db/models/base.py, during _save_table(), we should change setattr(self, field.attname, value) to setattr(self, field.attname, field.to_python(value)). We should also make a similar update in django/db/models/query.py within bulk_create where results from _batched_insert are processed, ensuring field.to_python is called before calling setattr on the objects.

I think the root cause of the database connection leaks is that the server is keeping connections alive via HTTP keep-alive, which prevents the request handling threads from exiting and releasing their database connections. We should disable keep-alive in WSGIRequestHandler to ensure connections are closed immediately after each request. We can do this by modifying WSGIRequestHandler.handle to always set self.close_connection = True, which will disable the keep-alive loop.

I think the root cause of the TypeError is that the `Exists` class (and other query expressions inheriting from `Combinable`) is missing the reflected operators `__rand__` and `__ror__`. Currently, `Exists(...) & Q(...)` works because `Exists` implements `__and__` via `Combinable`, but when `Q` is on the left-hand side like `Q(...) & Exists(...)`, Python needs to fall back to the right-hand side operator on `Exists`. We should update `Combinable` in `django/db/models/expressions.py` to implement `__rand__` and `__ror__` so they can handle being combined with `Q` objects.

I think the root cause of this issue is in the `clean` method of `MultiValueField` in `django/forms/fields.py`. When a form is submitted with all subfields empty and the parent `MultiValueField` has `required=False`, the method returns early with `self.compress([])` at line 1029. This bypasses the validation loop that checks individual subfields. We should remove this early return when `self.required` is `False` so that the method falls through to the loop where each subfield's `required` status is correctly evaluated. This will ensure that if a subfield is marked as `required=True`, validation will fail as expected even if the parent field itself is optional.

I think the duplicate yields occur because the same file is being processed multiple times within each post-processing pass loop. We should introduce a yielded set inside the pass loop in post_process to track which files have been yielded during that pass, and only yield them if they haven't been yielded yet in the current pass.

I think the issue is that OrderedSet doesn't support the reversed() built-in because it doesn't implement the __reversed__ method. Since OrderedSet stores its elements in an underlying dictionary (self.dict), we should implement __reversed__(self) to return reversed(self.dict.values()) to retrieve the reversed elements of the set.

I think the root cause is that `QuerySet.values()` does not clear the model's default ordering when it is used in conjunction with annotations. We should update the `values()` method in `django/db/models/query.py` to check if the query will perform aggregation, and if so, clear the default ordering by calling `self.query.clear_ordering(force_empty=True)` before returning the cloned queryset. This will ensure that default ordering fields do not end up in the GROUP BY clause.

I think the root cause is that `Q.deconstruct()` assumes its children are always key-value pairs when there is only one child, which fails when combining `Q` objects with non-subscriptable boolean expressions like `Exists`. We should keep the special case for single-child `Q` objects to maintain backward compatibility, but add an explicit check to make sure the child is a length-2 tuple before trying to deconstruct it into `kwargs`. If it's not a tuple of length 2, we should deconstruct it into `args` instead.

I think we should unwrap functools.partial objects in ResolverMatch.__init__() to handle them nicely. If the passed func is an instance of functools.partial, we can set self.func to func.func, and then merge func.args and func.keywords into self.args and self.kwargs. This ensures the underlying view is correctly stored and its pre-bound arguments are accessible, which should resolve the issues with repr showing functools.partial generically.

I think the root cause is that `YearLookup` does not calculate the correct boundaries for ISO week-numbering years. We should update `year_lookup_bounds_for_date_field` and `year_lookup_bounds_for_datetime_field` in `django/db/backends/base/operations.py` to use `datetime.date.fromisocalendar` and `datetime.datetime.fromisocalendar` respectively. The bounds for an ISO year should start at week 1, day 1 of the year, and end at week 52, day 7 of that year to cover the standard 52 weeks.

I think the root cause of the ValueError is in `django/db/models/options.py` within the `_get_default_pk_class` method. The check `issubclass(pk_class, AutoField)` is too restrictive because it doesn't account for subclasses of `BigAutoField` or `SmallAutoField` which do not inherit from `AutoField` in their Python MRO. We should update `django/db/models/options.py` to import `BigAutoField` and `SmallAutoField` and modify the check to `issubclass(pk_class, (AutoField, BigAutoField, SmallAutoField))` to support these custom primary key classes.

I think the root cause is that `__main__.__spec__.parent` is not always set (for example, when running top-level modules that are not part of a package). When it is set, we should definitely use it to ensure the process runs in the correct package context. We should update `django/utils/autoreload.py` in `get_child_arguments()` to check if `__main__.__spec__.parent` is present. If it is, we use it with `-m`; otherwise, we should fallback to `__main__.__spec__.name`.

I think the root cause is that the postgresql client's runshell method in django/db/backends/postgresql/client.py does not correctly handle cases where the environment dictionary returned by settings_to_cmd_args_env is empty. We should update runshell in the PostgreSQL client to check if env is empty and, if so, populate it with os.environ before calling super().runshell, or handle the subprocess execution directly there with the merged environment.

I think we should refactor URLValidator.__call__ to split the URL using urlsplit() at the very beginning. This will allow us to validate the scheme and handle IDN conversion on the netloc component upfront, before running the main regex validation on the reconstructed URL. This simplifies the flow and avoids having to catch ValidationError just to handle IDNs.

I think the root cause is that when `Q` objects are combined using `OR`, the subqueries inside `In` lookups do not get their `subquery` attribute set to `True` during expression resolution. This causes the compiler to treat them as normal queries and include all default columns in the `GROUP BY` clause. We should update `WhereNode.resolve_expression` in `django/db/models/sql/where.py` to ensure that all nested queries in `OR` branches have `subquery = True` explicitly set.

I think the root cause is that `DateFormat.Y()` returns the year as an integer instead of a formatted string, relying on the formatter to convert it. We should update `DateFormat.Y()` to use the standard library's `strftime` method to ensure it is properly formatted as a 4-digit year string, like `return self.data.strftime('%Y')`.

I think the deprecation warnings are coming from the `mysqlclient` driver connection calls, which are managed in `django/db/backends/mysql/base.py`. We should update `get_connection_params` to use `database` instead of `db` and `password` instead of `passwd`. The `django/db/backends/mysql/client.py` file only handles generating command-line arguments for the `mysql` CLI tool and doesn't use `mysqlclient`, so we don't need to modify it.

I think the root cause is that `catch_all_view` is using `request.path_info` to resolve and redirect, which strips the script prefix. We should update `catch_all_view` to use `request.path` instead of `request.path_info` when constructing the `path` variable. This will ensure that the redirect URL includes the script prefix when `FORCE_SCRIPT_NAME` or `SCRIPT_NAME` is used.

I think the root cause of this issue is that `TableColumns` in `django/db/backends/ddl_references.py` is initialized with a `Table` instance instead of a string table name in some execution paths. This causes the comparison `self.table == table` in `TableColumns.references_column` to fail when it expects a string. We should update `TableColumns.__init__` to ensure `self.table` is stored as a string by calling `str(table)` so that the comparison works correctly.

I think the root cause is that `post_process` is attempting to run when `max_post_process_passes` is set to 0. If the user explicitly sets `max_post_process_passes = 0`, it means they want to disable the post-processing phase entirely. We should check this condition at the beginning of `post_process` in `django/contrib/staticfiles/storage.py` and return early to avoid the `UnboundLocalError` and skip unnecessary work.

I think the issue is that we are marking the replaced migrations as unapplied instead of the squashed migration itself during the unapply process. In django/db/migrations/executor.py, inside the unapply_migration method, when migration.replaces is populated, we loop through and record each replaced migration as unapplied. We should instead only record the squashed migration itself (using migration.app_label and migration.name) as unapplied, as it is the migration currently in the graph. We don't need to individually mark the replaced migrations as unapplied.

I think the root cause is that `BoundWidget.id_for_label` doesn't check if the ID is already present in the subwidget's attributes. We should update `BoundWidget.id_for_label` in `django/forms/boundfield.py` to use `self.data['attrs'].get('id')` if it exists. However, to ensure backward compatibility and avoid breaking cases where the ID might not be set in `attrs`, we should fall back to the current default format `id_%s_%s` using `self.data['attrs'].get('id', 'id_%s_%s' % (self.data['name'], self.data['index']))`.

I think the root cause is that `trim_punctuation` calculates the slice index for the escaped string `middle` using the length of the unescaped `stripped` string, which causes an index mismatch when HTML entities are present. We should update `trim_punctuation` to calculate the length of the stripped text after escaping it, so we can correctly slice `middle`. We can do this by using `len(escape(stripped))` to determine the new end of `middle` and the start of `trail`.

I think we can get the number of updated rows by tracking the number of objects we attempt to update in each batch. We should initialize a counter before the loop and increment it by `len(pks)` for each batch, then return it at the end of `bulk_update()`. This seems safer than relying on the database-specific return values of the individual `update()` calls.

I think the root cause is in `django/db/migrations/writer.py`. When a migration contains a `CreateModel` operation, its base classes (like `models.Model`) are serialized as a tuple, but `MigrationWriter` doesn't know to include `from django.db import models` in the generated imports list because the bases are formatted dynamically in `OperationWriter` as part of the operation string. We should check if the generated `operations` string in `MigrationWriter.as_string()` contains "models.Model", and if so, append 'from django.db import models' to the imports set so that the generated migration code will import the `models` module correctly.

I think we should update the `non_form_errors` method in `django/forms/formsets.py` to set the `error_class` attribute of `self._non_form_errors` to `'nonform'` before returning it. This avoids having to pass `error_class` during initialization in multiple places inside `full_clean`.

I think the inconsistency between `BaseForm._clean_fields()` and `BoundField.initial` for disabled fields with callable initials should be resolved by accessing the initial value directly from `self.initial` (or falling back to `field.initial`) within `_clean_fields()`, rather than refactoring it to use `BoundField` objects. `BoundField` is primarily designed for the template/presentation layer, and using it within the form cleaning lifecycle could introduce unnecessary coupling. We just need to make sure we evaluate the callable correctly when retrieving it from `self.initial` or `field.initial` in `_clean_fields()`.

I think the root cause is in `django/db/models/base.py` in `_check_field_name_clashes`. The check `if f not in used_fields:` is comparing a field/relation object `f` against the keys of `used_fields`, which are strings (field names/attnames). This triggers a hash look-up on `f` (which fails when it is a `ManyToManyRel` with a list for `through_fields`). We should update this check to `if f.name not in used_fields:` to avoid hashing the relation object.

I think we can implement the `edit_only` feature by updating `modelformset_factory` and `inlineformset_factory` to accept an `edit_only` parameter (defaulting to `False`). If `edit_only` is `True`, we should set `extra=0` to prevent any new blank forms from being displayed. This should be sufficient to restrict the formset to editing existing objects.
