I think we should support extra fields by allowing the related model to define a method `to_autocomplete()` that returns the serialized representation. In `AutocompleteJsonView.get`, we can check if this method exists on the object and use it, falling back to the default `{'id': ..., 'text': ...}` representation if it doesn't. This keeps the model's presentation logic encapsulated within the model itself and avoids the need to subclass `AutocompleteJsonView` just to add extra fields.

I think we should make ProjectState.__init__ more robust by ensuring real_apps is always converted to a set if it is not None, to maintain backward compatibility with third-party migrations that might pass lists or tuples. We should update the initialization in django/db/migrations/state.py to safely convert it using set(real_apps) instead of asserting it is a set.

I think the root cause is that the child process command line is reconstructed in `django/utils/autoreload.py` inside `get_child_arguments()`, but it fails to propagate interpreter options like `-X`. We should update `get_child_arguments()` to parse `sys.argv` for any arguments starting with `-X` and append them to the reconstructed arguments list so they are passed to the child process.

I think the root cause is that `functools.partial` objects do not have standard function attributes like `__name__` or `__module__`, which causes decorators that use `functools.wraps` to fail when applied to them. We should avoid using `functools.partial` in `_multi_decorate` (inside `django/utils/decorators.py`) and instead define a standard wrapper function to bind the method to the instance. This wrapper function will have the necessary function attributes by default, preventing the `AttributeError`.

I think the root cause is that `timezone._get_timezone_name()` returns the string representation of the timezone, which for standard `datetime.timezone` objects (like those returned by `get_fixed_timezone()` when `pytz` is not used) contains the 'UTC' prefix (e.g., 'UTC+10:00') instead of the raw offset. We should check if the timezone is an instance of `datetime.timezone` and return `timezone.tzname(None)` to get the clean offset, falling back to `str(timezone)` for other timezone types.

I think the root cause is that `reverse` is unable to resolve URLs for custom admin sites because it defaults to the 'admin' namespace. To fix this without affecting the default admin, we should check if the admin site is the default 'admin' site. If it is, we can continue using `reverse`. Otherwise, for custom admin sites, we should manually construct the URL path using the site's name as the prefix, like `f'/{self.model_admin.admin_site.name}/{remote_field.model._meta.app_label}/{remote_field.model._meta.model_name}/{quote(remote_obj.pk)}/change/'` in `get_admin_url`.

I think the root cause is that `ModelChoiceIteratorValue` defines `__eq__` but lacks `__hash__`, making it unhashable. We should implement `__hash__` in `ModelChoiceIteratorValue` to return `hash(id(self))` so that it behaves like a standard object and can be hashed.

I think the root cause is that we are calling `schema_editor.alter_db_table` in `RenameModel.database_forwards` without checking if the table name actually changes. When `db_table` is explicitly defined, the old and new models will have the same table name. We should update `database_forwards` to compare `old_model._meta.db_table` and `new_model._meta.db_table`, and skip the `alter_db_table` call if they are equal, allowing the migration to proceed with updating the references in the state and related fields without renaming the table.

I think the root cause is that get_search_results applies the search filters sequentially inside a loop using queryset = queryset.filter(or_queries). When search fields involve multi-valued relationships, each call to filter() forces the Django ORM to generate a new SQL JOIN. To resolve this performance bottleneck and prevent the query from stalling, we should pre-evaluate which fields in search_fields are relations, and apply prefetch_related to the queryset before looping over the search terms. This will ensure that the related tables are cached and Django can resolve the filters without spawning duplicate joins for each search term.

I think the root cause is that inspectdb doesn't handle cases where the foreign key column name in the source table differs from the referenced column name in the target table. We should compare the local column name with the referenced column name returned by relations[column_name][0]. If they differ, we should set db_column in extra_params to the referenced column name to ensure the relationship is mapped correctly.

I think the root cause is that `to_locale` in `django/utils/translation/__init__.py` does not correctly format language codes containing both script and region. It currently converts `en-latn-us` to `en_Latn-us` instead of `en_Latn_US`. This mixed format (using both underscores and dashes) is inconsistent with standard locale formats and causes the translation lookup to fail. We should update `to_locale` to ensure all parts after the language code are joined by underscores, and that the region part is correctly uppercase, yielding `en_Latn_US`.

I think the root cause is that the json_script template filter in django/template/defaultfilters.py requires the element_id argument. We should update the filter definition to make element_id optional by defaulting it to None (i.e., def json_script(value, element_id=None):). We don't need to modify the underlying django.utils.html.json_script function because it is a low-level utility and changing its signature might break backwards compatibility for python code that calls it. The template filter will pass None to the utility function, and format_html will handle it.

I think the root cause is that custom ForeignKey fields that remove 'to' from their deconstructed kwargs are violating Django's model field contract. Instead of making the autodetector more lenient by using pop(), we should enforce that relation fields must include 'to' in their deconstruction. We should add a validation check in `ForeignKey.check` to verify that 'to' is present in the deconstructed kwargs and raise a validation error if it is missing.

I think the root cause is that `LEVEL_TAGS` in `django/contrib/messages/storage/base.py` is initialized at import time and doesn't get updated when settings are overridden. We should update `LEVEL_TAGS` dynamically in the `MessageMiddleware.process_request` method to ensure it reflects the overridden settings for each request.

I think the root cause of the `AssertionError` in `Query.change_aliases` is that `Query.combine` incorrectly allows join reuse when combining queries with `OR` (using `reuse = set(self.alias_map)`). This reuse leads to overlapping alias maps when merging the right-hand side joins, which eventually causes `change_map` keys to intersect with its values. We should update `Query.combine` to disable join reuse for `OR` queries by setting `reuse = set()` unconditionally, similar to how we handle `AND` queries. This will ensure that RHS joins are assigned fresh aliases and prevent the conflict in `change_map`.

I think we can simplify the deconstruction of all expression subclasses by implementing a custom `deconstruct` method on the base `Expression` class in `django/db/models/expressions.py`, rather than decorating each subclass individually. Since `Expression` is already marked as `@deconstructible`, we can just override `deconstruct` to dynamically return the path under `django.db.models` using `self.__class__.__name__`.

I think the root cause is that `MigrationRecorder` does not check the database router before creating the `django_migrations` table. We should update `MigrationRecorder.ensure_schema` in `django/db/migrations/recorder.py` to check `router.allow_migrate` for the `Migration` model on the current connection. If the router returns `False`, we should skip creating the table. Similarly, we should check it in `record_applied` and `record_unapplied` to avoid database errors when trying to write to a table that doesn't exist.

I think the root cause is that `ModelOptionOperation.reduce` is too restrictive. It uses `isinstance(operation, (self.__class__, DeleteModel))` to check if it can collapse operations. Since `AlterUniqueTogether` and `AlterIndexTogether` are different classes (even though they both inherit from `AlterTogetherOptionOperation` / `ModelOptionOperation`), the optimizer cannot collapse them together. We should update the check in `django/db/migrations/operations/models.py` inside `ModelOptionOperation.reduce` to use `ModelOptionOperation` instead of `self.__class__` so that different option operations on the same model can be correctly optimized into a single operation.

I think the root cause of the TypeError is that `Value._resolve_output_field` returns a `CharField` instance with `max_length` set to `None`. Since `CharField` expects a valid `max_length` to construct its validators, we should update `Value._resolve_output_field` to instantiate `CharField` with `max_length` set to the length of the string value (i.e., `max_length=len(self.value)`). This will ensure that `MaxLengthValidator` is initialized with a proper integer limit, preventing the comparison crash when `clean()` is called.

I think the root cause is that SQLite's schema editor doesn't support adding UNIQUE columns directly via `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` during migrations. To fix this, we should catch the `unique` flag in `django/db/backends/sqlite3/schema.py`'s `add_field` method, temporarily set `field._unique` to `False` to let `super().add_field` append the column without the `UNIQUE` inline constraint, and then add a deferred `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` statement using `self.execute(self._create_unique_sql(model, [field]))`.

I think the root cause is in `django/db/models/fields/related_descriptors.py` within `ForwardManyToOneDescriptor.__get__`. The descriptor is returning a cached instance of the parent object that was loaded with deferred fields from the outer query, ignoring the fact that a nested prefetch has already loaded a more complete instance. We should update `ForwardManyToOneDescriptor.__get__` to check if the cached object has deferred fields using `get_deferred_fields()`, and if so, bypass the cache to fetch a fresh instance that includes the prefetched fields.

I think the root cause is that Field.__hash__() is being evaluated before the model class is fully registered and the app registry is ready. We should update __hash__ to check if the app registry is ready via self.model._meta.apps.ready before including the model's app_label and model_name in the hash. This should ensure we only use stable model identifiers for the hash.

I think the root cause is that bulk_update does not extract the field name from F expressions before updating. We should check if the attribute is an instance of F, extract its name, and wrap it in a Value object, like: if isinstance(attr, F): attr = Value(attr.name, output_field=field). This will ensure the field name is correctly passed to the update query.

I think the issue is that wrapping the aggregate expression in `Coalesce` (which happens when `default` is provided) confuses the query compiler when there are existing annotations. Specifically, in `Aggregate.resolve_expression`, we return a `Coalesce` instance. If the query already has annotations, we shouldn't mark this `Coalesce` wrapper as a summary because the annotations will force a subquery. We should update `Aggregate.resolve_expression` to only set `is_summary` on the `Coalesce` instance if there are no existing annotations on the query (i.e. check `query.annotations`).

I think the issue is that when a model is renamed, its old name is no longer present in `to_state.models`, causing a `KeyError` when we try to look up `new_model_state` in `generate_renamed_fields`. We should add a safeguard check to verify if the `old_model_name` exists in `self.to_state.models` before trying to access it, and if it's missing, we should simply skip detecting renamed fields for that model in this iteration.

I think the root cause is that the `Exists` expression inherits `empty_result_set_value = None` from `Subquery`. For `Exists`, an empty subquery should evaluate to `False` (or `True` if negated) instead of `None`. We should update `Exists` in `django/db/models/expressions.py` to implement `empty_result_set_value` as a property that returns `not self.negated` so that the compiler can resolve it correctly when the subquery is empty.

I think the root cause of this issue is in the `AdminRadioSelect` widget (defined in `django/contrib/admin/widgets.py`). When a ForeignKey field uses `radio_fields`, Django switches the widget to `AdminRadioSelect`. However, the widget itself does not receive or respect the `empty_label` override from the field or ModelAdmin. We should modify `AdminRadioSelect` to accept an `empty_label` parameter in its constructor and use it when rendering the choices, rather than trying to fix it in `options.py` which is just responsible for field configuration.

I think we should implement the optimization in `AlterModelManagers.reduce` since it's the `AlterModelManagers` operation that we want to eliminate. We should check if the other operation is `CreateModel` and, if so, merge the managers.

I think the root cause is that the `KeyTransform` class's database-specific methods, such as `as_sqlite`, `as_mysql`, and `as_oracle`, do not correctly distinguish between numeric keys and array indexes when compiling the JSON path. We should update these methods to check if the key is a numeric string and, if so, explicitly format it as an object key (e.g., using the `.\"key\"` syntax) rather than allowing `compile_json_path` to default it to an array index bracket notation.

I think the root cause of the `DoesNotExist` exception during `loaddata` on a non-default database is that the `natural_key()` method on the model does not receive any database context, so it cannot forward the database alias when resolving its dependencies. We should update the `natural_key()` method signature across our models to accept an optional `using` database alias (e.g., `def natural_key(self, using=None)`) and pass this parameter when resolving related natural keys, like `self.author.natural_key(using=using)`. Then, in `django/core/serializers/base.py`, we should update `build_instance` to pass the database alias when calling `natural_key()`: `natural_key = Model(**data).natural_key(using=db)`.

I think the root cause is in `django/db/models/sql/datastructures.py`. The `Join.equals` method has a comment saying `# Ignore filtered_relation in equality check.` and indeed it ignores it: `return self.identity[:-1] == other.identity[:-1]`. This is why multiple `FilteredRelation` on the same relation reuse the same join, because the equality check doesn't distinguish them based on their filtered relation. We should update `Join.equals` to compare the full `self.identity` including `filtered_relation` so that joins with different filtered relations are not incorrectly reused.

I think the root cause is that the `AlterField` migration operation does not optimize out changes that only affect Python-level attributes like `choices`. We should modify `database_forwards` in `django/db/migrations/operations/fields.py` to compare `from_field` and `to_field`. If only `choices` (or other non-database attributes) have changed, we should skip calling `schema_editor.alter_field` entirely to avoid triggering database alterations, which is especially expensive on SQLite where it rebuilds the table.

I think the root cause is that we are filtering the parent update query by the child's primary keys directly, which doesn't work when the child inherits from multiple parents with different primary keys. Instead, we should filter the parent query by referencing the child relation. We should update `get_related_updates` in `django/db/models/sql/subqueries.py` to use `query.add_filter(f"{self.model._meta.model_name}__in", self.related_ids)` instead of `query.add_filter("pk__in", self.related_ids)`.

I think the root cause is that `_unregister_lookup` only removes the lookup from the class it is directly called on, but doesn't propagate this removal to subclasses' `class_lookups` dictionaries. We should update `_unregister_lookup` to recursively iterate through all subclasses using `subclasses(cls)` and delete the lookup from their `class_lookups` if present. We should avoid calling `_clear_cached_lookups()` here as it would discard the entire lookup cache and cause performance issues; instead, we should surgically clean up the dictionaries.

I think the root cause is in `django/template/autoreload.py` inside the `template_changed` receiver. When an empty string is present in `TEMPLATES['DIRS']`, it gets normalized to the project's root directory. This causes `template_changed` to match any file change within the project because `template_dir` (which is now the project root) will be a parent of almost every file path. We should update `template_changed` to check if `template_dir` is equal to the project root (e.g., `Path.cwd()`) and skip it to prevent this false positive match.

I think the root cause of the foreign key constraint errors is that the schema editor does not propagate collation changes to referencing foreign keys when a primary key is altered. We should update `_alter_field` in `django/db/backends/base/schema.py` to check if the primary key's collation has changed during an alteration. If it has, we can iterate through the related models in the `rels_to_update` loop and manually apply the new collation to the referencing foreign key columns using `_alter_column_collation_sql` on them. This will ensure that the database schema remains consistent.

I think the root cause is that we are not checking if the old index name is the same as the new index name before renaming. We should update `RenameIndex.database_forwards` to check if `self.old_name` is equal to `self.new_name` and return early if they are equal, to avoid trying to rename an index to its current name.

I think the root cause is that the dynamically generated manager methods in `BaseManager._get_queryset_methods` do not copy the signature-related attributes from the original queryset methods. We should update `create_method` in `django/db/models/manager.py` to manually copy `__annotations__`, `__defaults__`, and `__kwdefaults__` from `method` to `manager_method` along with `__name__` and `__doc__`. This will ensure that `inspect.signature()` can correctly reconstruct the signature including default values and type annotations.

I think the root cause is that when dropping a unique_together constraint, the schema editor searches for all unique constraints on the column. If the field is a primary key, it will find both the primary key constraint and the unique_together constraint, leading to a ValueError because it expects only one constraint. We should update the `alter_unique_together` method in `django/db/backends/base/schema.py` to pass `primary_key=False` inside the constraint kwargs to `_delete_composed_index` so that the primary key constraint is ignored and only the unique_together constraint is returned.

I think the root cause is that `date_format` and `time_format` in `django/utils/formats.py` do not handle lazy string arguments for the `format` parameter. When they receive a lazy string (for example, from a template filter like `some_date|date:_('Y-m-d')`), they pass it directly to `get_format`, which then fails. We should update `date_format` and `time_format` to convert the `format` argument to a string if it is not None.

I think the root cause is that `RelatedPopulator` fails to locate the primary key in `init_list` when working with proxy models because it searches using the proxy model's metadata. We should modify `RelatedPopulator.__init__` in `django/db/models/query.py` to resolve the PK against the concrete model using `self.model_cls._meta.concrete_model._meta.pk.attname`. If the resolved PK attribute name is still missing from `self.init_list`, we should append it to the list to ensure `self.pk_idx` can be correctly determined.

I think we should update the runshell method in django/db/backends/postgresql/client.py to post-process the arguments. Since settings_to_cmd_args_env is a helper method, the actual execution order should be managed in runshell. We can call settings_to_cmd_args_env with empty parameters to get the base command and dbname, and then insert the parameters before the dbname in runshell before passing them to subprocess.run.

I think the root cause is that `django/utils/numberformat.py`'s `format` function doesn't handle decimal formatting for string inputs correctly. In `floatformat` filter, after converting the value to a string, we call `formats.number_format` which delegates to `numberformat.format`. If we look at `django/utils/numberformat.py`, the Decimal-specific formatting (which handles high precision and avoids scientific notation issues) is only triggered if `isinstance(number, Decimal)`. Since we pass a string `number` from `floatformat`, it falls into the `else` block and is treated as a regular string, which bypasses the Decimal checks and causes precision loss. We should update `django/utils/numberformat.py` to attempt converting string inputs to `Decimal` so they can benefit from the high-precision formatting logic.

I think the root cause is in ModelFormMetaclass.__new__, which fails to inspect the Meta class of the form being defined for the formfield_callback attribute. Currently, it only checks the base classes' Meta or a class-level formfield_callback attribute. We should update ModelFormMetaclass.__new__ to extract formfield_callback from attrs['Meta'] if it is defined there, before falling back to base_formfield_callback.

I think the root cause is in `Case.as_sql` in `django/db/models/expressions.py`. When a condition like `~Q(pk__in=[])` matches everything, it compiles to an empty string. During `Case.as_sql` evaluation, this results in compiling a `When` expression to `WHEN  THEN ...`, leading to the `ProgrammingError: syntax error at or near "THEN"`. We should inspect the compiled SQL of each case in the loop inside `Case.as_sql` and skip cases where the condition's compiled SQL is empty (or matches a blank structure like `WHEN  THEN`) to avoid generating malformed SQL.

I think the root cause is that QuerySet.filter blocks filtering on sliced querysets to prevent database-level mismatches. We should resolve this by allowing sliced querysets to be filtered during prefetch. We can achieve this in django/db/models/fields/related_descriptors.py by temporarily clearing the slice limits on the queryset, applying the relation filter, and then re-applying the slice limits on the resulting queryset within the get_prefetch_queryset methods.

I think the root cause is that during migration execution, the `through` model on the many-to-many field is still a string reference if it is defined in another app and hasn't been resolved yet. When `schema_editor.create_model` attempts to inspect `field.remote_field.through._meta.auto_created`, it fails because the string hasn't been replaced with the actual model class. We should update `django/db/backends/base/schema.py` to check if `through` is a string and, if so, resolve it using the state's apps registry or simply bypass the `auto_created` check if it cannot be resolved yet.

I think the root cause is that settings.FIXTURE_DIRS can contain a mix of string paths and pathlib.Path instances, leading to type mismatch during comparisons. We should update the fixture_dirs method in django/core/management/commands/loaddata.py to normalize the directories by converting all elements in fixture_dirs = settings.FIXTURE_DIRS into pathlib.Path objects. This ensures that we have a consistent type for all directory paths we are working with.

I think the root cause is in `RelatedIn.get_prep_lookup` in `django/db/models/fields/related_lookups.py`. When `QuerySet.alias()` is used, it incorrectly flags the RHS query as having select fields (`has_select_fields` becomes `True`), preventing `RelatedIn.get_prep_lookup` from clearing the select clause. We should update the condition in `RelatedIn.get_prep_lookup` to check if `self.rhs.select` is empty, indicating that no explicit fields were selected, and if so, clear the select clause. Specifically, we should change the condition from `not getattr(self.rhs, "has_select_fields", True)` to `(not getattr(self.rhs, "has_select_fields", True) or not self.rhs.select)`.

I think the root cause is that database backends do not properly format mixed-type division operations for the MOD operator. We should update the `combine_expression` method in the SQLite backend (`django/db/backends/sqlite3/operations.py`) and other relevant backends (like `django/db/backends/base/operations.py`) to cast one of the operands when mixing Float, Decimal, or Integer with the MOD operator ('%%').

I think the root cause of unexpected states is that individual object updates within the bulk-edit loop in `changelist_view` are not isolated. We should wrap the save operations for each changed form in `transaction.atomic` using the database router for the model. This ensures that a failure in saving one object (or its related objects) rolls back only that object's changes, preventing database corruption for that specific record while allowing the rest of the bulk edit to proceed.

I think the root cause is that `makemigrations` is writing files when the `--check` flag is active. We should update the `handle` method in `django/core/management/commands/makemigrations.py` to check the `check_changes` option inside the `else` block (when changes are detected). If `check_changes` is True, we should just return early to prevent the migration files from being written.

I think the root cause is that the `http_method_not_allowed` method in `django/views/generic/base.py` is defined as a synchronous function. When an async view receives an unsupported request method, Django attempts to await the response from `http_method_not_allowed`, which results in a TypeError because it returns a sync HttpResponseNotAllowed object instead of a coroutine. We should update `http_method_not_allowed` to be an async function using `async def` so that it returns a coroutine that can be successfully awaited.

I think the root cause is that the password change view in `UserAdmin` doesn't handle `to_field` lookups. When `UserAdmin` is accessed via a relation with `to_field` set (e.g., `to_field="uuid"`), the URL contains the UUID instead of the PK. However, `UserAdmin.user_change_password` calls `self.get_object(request, unquote(id))` without passing the `to_field` parameter, so it defaults to PK lookup and fails with a 404. We should update `user_change_password` in `django/contrib/auth/admin.py` to check for `_to_field` in the request parameters and pass it to `get_object` like this:

```python
to_field = request.POST.get(TO_FIELD_VAR, request.GET.get(TO_FIELD_VAR))
user = self.get_object(request, unquote(id), to_field)
```
This will allow the view to correctly resolve the user using the alternative field provided in the URL context.

I think the root cause is that the WSGI server in `django/core/servers/basehttp.py` does not resolve the shorthand '0' address to '0.0.0.0' during initialization. We should update the `run` function in `django/core/servers/basehttp.py` to normalize the address '0' to '0.0.0.0' before passing it to the server class, ensuring it binds to all interfaces correctly.

I think the root cause is that when `lastmod` is callable and the sitemap contains no items, `get_latest_lastmod` raises a `ValueError` because it tries to call `max()` on an empty list of evaluated `lastmod` dates. We should update `django/contrib/sitemaps/__init__.py` to check if the sitemap is empty (by calling `self.items()`), and if so, return `self.lastmod` as the default fallback value instead of evaluating the callable across empty items.

I think we should focus on the related managers in `django/db/models/fields/related_descriptors.py` as pointed out in the report. We need to add `acreate`, `aget_or_create`, and `aupdate_or_create` to both `RelatedManager` (in `create_reverse_many_to_one_manager`) and `ManyRelatedManager` (in `create_forward_many_to_many_manager`). By defining these methods to wrap their respective synchronous versions with `sync_to_async`, we ensure the manager-specific logic is executed instead of falling back to the default `QuerySet` implementation.

I think the root cause is that non-aggregate annotations are being unnecessarily included in count queries, which can lead to inefficient SQL or incorrect subqueries. We should update `get_aggregation` in `django/db/models/sql/query.py` to identify annotations that do not contain aggregates (by checking if `getattr(annotation, 'contains_aggregate', False)` is False) and remove them from `self.annotations` before we determine if a subquery is needed. We should keep aggregate annotations as they are necessary for grouping and aggregation logic.

I think the root cause is that `SQLInsertCompiler.as_sql` uses the raw field names passed to `bulk_create` for `update_fields` and `unique_fields`. We should resolve these to their database attribute names using `self.query.model._meta.get_field(name).attname` before passing them to `on_conflict_suffix_sql` to ensure we use the correct database-level names.

I think the root cause is that UserCreationForm.save bypasses the standard ModelForm saving mechanism by directly accessing self.instance and saving it, which prevents many-to-many fields from being processed. We should update UserCreationForm.save to first call super().save(commit=False) to properly initialize the user instance and set up any necessary saving hooks, then set the password on the returned user, and finally save the user instance if commit=True.

I think the root cause is that `timesince` doesn't align the timezones of the input datetimes before calculating the delta. When `USE_TZ=True`, the inputs `d` and `now` can have different timezone offsets. We should update `timesince` to ensure that if both `d` and `now` are timezone-aware, we convert `d` to the timezone of `now` using `d.astimezone(now.tzinfo)` before we perform the subtraction.

I think the root cause of the traceback is that `parser.parse_args(argv[2:])` in `BaseCommand.run_from_argv` is called outside of the `try...except CommandError` block. When a subparser fails to validate arguments, it raises a `CommandError` which escapes uncaught. We should update `BaseCommand.run_from_argv` in `django/core/management/base.py` to wrap both `parser.parse_args` and `self.execute` in the same `try...except CommandError` block to ensure all parsing errors are caught and printed cleanly to stderr.

I think the root cause of the ValueError: valid range for prec is [1, MAX_PREC] crash is that when floatformat receives a mathematically zero value with trailing zeros (like Decimal('0.00')) and we ask for 0 decimal places (p=0), the precision calculation prec = abs(p) + units + 1 results in 0. Since the value is mathematically zero, we don't need to perform any quantization. We should add a check at the beginning of the function: if d == 0: return mark_safe(formats.number_format('0', 0)) to bypass the quantization logic and return '0' immediately.

I think the root cause is that FileField.deconstruct does not check if the storage itself is a callable before comparing it to default_storage. We should update deconstruct to check if self.storage is callable, and if so, use it directly as the storage keyword argument instead of checking if it is default_storage.

I think the root cause of the issue is that Django's `ConditionalGetMiddleware` in `django/middleware/http.py` is bypassing HEAD requests. We should update the middleware to process both GET and HEAD requests, and if the request method is HEAD, we should clear the response content while keeping the headers intact. This will ensure that HEAD requests return empty bodies consistently.

I think we should update changeform_view in django/contrib/admin/options.py to address this. Since 'save as new' is an add operation, we should check if the user has add permission using self.has_add_permission(request). If they do not, we can disable the feature for this view by setting self.save_as = False, which will automatically prevent the 'Save as new' button from being rendered in the submit row.

I think we should use the constraint's `name` as the `code` for the `ValidationError` raised during validation, rather than introducing a new `violation_error_code` attribute. Constraints are already required to have a unique name, which serves as a natural and descriptive identifier for the violation. Introducing `violation_error_code` adds unnecessary complexity to the constructors, `deconstruct()` serialization, equality checks, and representations across all constraint types (including contrib Postgres constraints). We can simply update the `validate()` methods to raise `ValidationError` with `code=self.name`.

I think the root cause is that `empty_form` passes `None` as the index to `add_fields`, which causes the comparison `index < initial_form_count` to fail with a `TypeError` when `can_delete_extra` is False. We should update `add_fields` to default `index` to `0` if it is `None` so that it has a valid integer index for comparison.

I think we need to modify `AlterField.reduce` in `django/db/migrations/operations/fields.py`. When optimizing migrations, if an `AlterField` is followed by another `AlterField` on the same field, the first operation should absorb the second one to avoid redundant database alterations. We should check if `operation` is an instance of `AlterField` and if it is the same field operation, and if so, return `[self]` to retain the initial alteration state.

I think the root cause is that AdminSite.catch_all_view() redirects using request.path, which drops the query string. We should use request.get_full_path() instead of request.path and append a trailing slash to it so that we preserve the query parameters during the redirect.

I think we should modify AbstractBaseUser.get_session_auth_hash to accept an optional secret argument, defaulting to None. If None, it should use the default settings.SECRET_KEY. In django/contrib/auth/__init__.py:get_user, if the constant_time_compare with the default hash fails, we should iterate over settings.SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS and verify the session hash against user.get_session_auth_hash(secret=fallback). If a match is found, we should allow the user to remain logged in.

I think the root cause is in django/views/static.py. When serving static files, the serve() view helper calls mimetypes.guess_type() which returns the uncompressed Content-Type (like 'text/html') along with the compression encoding ('br' or 'compress'). Because this guessed Content-Type is passed directly to FileResponse, FileResponse uses it as-is and cannot correct it. We should update django/views/static.py to check the guessed encoding and override the content_type to 'application/x-brotli' for 'br' or 'application/x-compress' for 'compress' before passing it to FileResponse.

I think the root cause of this issue is that `ModelAdmin.lookup_allowed()` incorrectly handles relations when the target field is the primary key, particularly when dealing with OneToOneFields. The existing check `field not in prev_field.path_infos[-1].target_fields` is overcomplicated and fails to resolve correctly in these scenarios. We should simplify this logic by directly checking if the field is the primary key of the model we are traversing. I think we should update the condition to `field is not model._meta.pk` to make the lookup validation more robust and clean.

I think the import sorting logic in `MigrationWriter.as_string` is unnecessarily complex. Instead of splitting the import strings and trying to sort by the module name with `key=lambda i: i.split()[1]`, we should just sort the import statements alphabetically as whole strings using `sorted(imports)`. This simplifies the code and should naturally group and sort them correctly.

I think the root cause is that `BaseTemporalField.to_python` in `django/forms/fields.py` does not handle `OverflowError` when validating temporal values. When a form is submitted with an excessively large integer for the year, the parsing of the date representation can raise an `OverflowError` which is not caught by the `except (ValueError, TypeError):` block in `to_python`. We should update `BaseTemporalField.to_python` to also catch `OverflowError` and raise a `ValidationError` with the message 'Enter a valid date.' to ensure it is handled gracefully.

I think the performance issue is due to `update_dimension_fields` performing checks even when `width_field` and `height_field` are not defined. We should optimize `update_dimension_fields` by checking if `self.width_field` and `self.height_field` are set at the very beginning of the method and returning immediately if they are not. This will avoid the overhead of checking for deferred fields and other operations when dimensions are not tracked, while keeping the signal handlers safely connected.

I think we should update `RemoveIndex` in `django/db/migrations/operations/models.py` by implementing a `reduce` method. Since `RemoveIndex` cancels out an `AddIndex` operation, we should check if the other operation is an instance of `AddIndex` targeting the same index name and model, and if so, return an empty list to optimize them away.

I think we should implement the `escapeseq` filter in `django/template/defaultfilters.py` by copying the pattern of the standard `escape` filter. Since it performs escaping, we should use the `@stringfilter` decorator to ensure the input is treated as a string before applying the filter, and then use `conditional_escape` on each element in the sequence.

I think the issue is that we are not passing enough information to the error constructor. We should update `_check_readonly_fields` to include the field name in the label. If we change line 755 to `"readonly_fields[%d] (%s)" % (index, field_name)`, the error message will automatically contain the field name. I checked and `_check_readonly_fields_item` just uses this label directly, so this is the simplest way to get the field name into the error output.

I think the root cause is that the fallback logic for XOR in `django/db/models/sql/where.py` is trying to use a math-based approach with `Case` and `Exact` which is hard to optimize and prone to errors. We should instead rewrite it to use a clean boolean expansion of the XOR operator. For multiple arguments, `a ^ b ^ c` should be converted to a combination of AND and OR clauses representing the condition where exactly one of the inputs is true: `(a AND NOT b AND NOT c) OR (NOT a AND b AND NOT c) OR (NOT a AND NOT b AND c)`. This is much more database-friendly and avoids using `Case` expressions.

I think the root cause is that we are calling `.only("pk")` in `queryset_iterator` for many-to-many fields when natural keys are not used. This conflicts with custom managers that use `select_related` on the related model because you cannot defer fields that are being traversed by `select_related`. Since we are just iterating over the related objects to get their primary keys, we should remove `.only("pk")` from `queryset_iterator` in both `django/core/serializers/python.py` and `django/core/serializers/xml_serializer.py`. This aligns with the natural keys code path which also doesn't restrict fields, and lets the manager's query run without raising conflicts.

I think the root cause is that `InlineForeignKeyField` validation is too strict when dealing with parent models that have auto-generated alternate keys (like UUIDFields with defaults). When adding a new instance, the parent's alternate key is temporarily set to `None` in `add_fields` to avoid validation issues, but `InlineForeignKeyField.clean()` still tries to validate against it. We should update `InlineForeignKeyField.clean()` to bypass validation or allow `None` values if the parent instance is new and the target field has a default value.

I think the root cause is that the `get_swappable_settings_name` cache becomes stale when settings are overridden in tests. We should connect a receiver to the `setting_changed` signal (specifically monitoring `AUTH_USER_MODEL` changes) that calls `apps.get_swappable_settings_name.cache_clear()`. This is cleaner than modifying `Apps.clear_cache` directly, as `clear_cache` should focus on registry-related cache invalidation rather than reacting to setting changes.

I think the root cause is that the SQL compiler does not correctly isolate window functions when they are nested inside aggregate functions in the SELECT clause. We should modify `SQLCompiler.get_select` in `django/db/models/sql/compiler.py` to detect when an annotation containing a window function (i.e., having `contains_over_clause=True`) is referenced by an aggregate. In such cases, the compiler should wrap the window function expression in an inline subquery during SQL generation to prevent PostgreSQL from raising a GroupingError.

I think the root cause is that `Field.deconstruct()` does not correctly handle class methods from nested classes when they are passed as the `default` argument. When `deconstruct()` returns the class method, the migration serializer tries to resolve it but loses the outer class context because it only has access to the method's immediate class via `__self__`, which does not contain the nesting information in its `__name__`. We should update `Field.deconstruct()` in `django/db/models/fields/__init__.py` to check if `self.default` is a bound method of a class (a class method) and if that class is nested. If so, we should manually construct the full path string using the class's `__qualname__` and return that as the `default` in the deconstructed keywords so it writes the correct path into the migration file.

I think the root cause is that `makemigrations` is performing consistency checks on all models returned by `apps.get_models(app_label)`, including unmanaged models. This leads to invalid combinations for routers that expect only managed models to be checked. We should update the check in `django/core/management/commands/makemigrations.py` to filter out unmanaged models by adding `if model._meta.managed` to the generator expression.

I think yielding Page objects directly in __iter__ might be too heavy and could lead to performance issues if the caller doesn't end up using all of them immediately, especially with large querysets. Instead, to keep it lightweight and consistent with how we currently use page_range, we should implement __iter__ on Paginator to return an iterator over the page numbers. We should update django/core/paginator.py to define __iter__ as returning iter(self.page_range).

I think the root cause is that `np.histogram` does not receive the `range` parameter when `density=True` because it needs to be passed explicitly rather than unpacked via `**hist_kwargs` when density is active. We should update the `np.histogram` call in `lib/matplotlib/axes/_axes.py` to explicitly pass `range=hist_kwargs.get('range')`.

I think the root cause is that `LogScale.limit_range_for_scale` in `lib/matplotlib/scale.py` does not handle inverted limits correctly. When the limits are inverted (i.e., `vmin > vmax`), they are not preserved during the limit range adjustment for the log scale. We should update `LogScale.limit_range_for_scale` to detect if the input limits are swapped, apply the positive range limits, and then swap them back before returning to preserve the inverted direction.

I think the root cause is that `LogNorm` is defined using `nonpositive="mask"` in `lib/matplotlib/colors.py`. When the image data contains negative values, they are masked, which eventually leads to an invalid `vmin` (like 0 or negative) during the resampling process in `_make_image`, causing the `ValueError: Invalid vmin or vmax`. We should change `LogNorm` to use `nonpositive="clip"` instead, which is the default for `LogScale`. This will safely clip non-positive values to a small positive number before the transform, preventing the invalid `vmin` and fixing the crash.

I think the root cause is that `ToolLineHandles.set_data` is receiving the initial default extents of `(0, 0)` and updating the line handles to 0, which forces the axes limits to include 0. We should update `ToolLineHandles.set_data` to ignore updates when the positions are both 0.

I think the root cause is that `Axes.clear` (via `cla()`) in `lib/matplotlib/axes/_base.py` fails to re-initialize the tick parameters from `rcParams` after clearing the axes. During `Axes.__init__`, tick properties like `xtick.top` and `xtick.labelbottom` are set from `rcParams`. However, when `clear()` is called, it clears the tick keyword arguments but doesn't re-apply these `rcParams` settings, causing them to fall back to hardcoded defaults in `Tick.__init__` (which explains why top/right ticks unexpectedly appear). We should refactor the tick parameter initialization block from `Axes.__init__` into a separate method and call it at the end of `Axes.cla()` to ensure the default style is correctly restored.

I think the issue is that `SubFigure` is missing a `legend` implementation, which makes it fall back to some incorrect default behavior or raise errors because it's not recognized as a full `Figure`. We should add a `legend` method directly to the `SubFigure` class in `lib/matplotlib/figure.py` that delegates to its parent figure: `def legend(self, *args, **kwargs): return self.figure.legend(*args, **kwargs)`. This way, we don't have to modify the core `Legend` class type checks in `legend.py` which are designed to work only with standard `Axes` or `Figure` objects.

I think the root cause of the spacing issue is that `_wrap_in_tex` in `lib/matplotlib/dates.py` does not handle colons and spaces, which TeX math mode then compresses or spaces incorrectly. We should update `_wrap_in_tex` to replace colons with `\\colon` and spaces with `\\ ` (a backslash followed by a space) to restore the correct spacing. This is cleaner than trying to escape them with braces and will work natively with TeX rendering.

I think the root cause is that `units.ConversionInterface.is_numlike` in `lib/matplotlib/units.py` does not properly handle empty iterables, causing it to return `None` (which is falsy, but it should be explicitly `False`). We should update `is_numlike` to explicitly return `False` if the input is an empty iterable. This will prevent the deprecation warning from being triggered when empty data is passed to categorical axes.

I think the issue is that when `extend='both'` is used with `drawedges=True`, the divider segments are being sliced too aggressively. In `lib/matplotlib/colorbar.py`, we should update the `_add_solids` method to check if `self.extend` is `'both'` and, if so, avoid slicing the segments with `[1:-1]` so that the extremity lines are preserved.

I think the root cause is that we are showing the offset for day-level ticks (level >= 2) which is redundant since the month and year should be clear from the plot context. We should update `format_ticks` in `lib/matplotlib/dates.py` to disable `show_offset` when `level >= 2` instead of `level < 2`.

I think the root cause is that `switch_backend` in `lib/matplotlib/pyplot.py` unconditionally closes all figures when called. When `get_backend()` is called after `rc_context` exits, it triggers `switch_backend` again with the default backend, which closes the figures created inside the context. We should update `switch_backend` to check if the requested backend is already the active one (by checking `_backend_mod`) and avoid calling `close('all')` if it matches, to prevent losing figures on redundant backend resolution.

I think the root cause is that calling `set_visible(False)` on a 3D Axes container (`Axes3D`) doesn't propagate the visibility status down to its internal components (the three coordinate axes and the background patch) which are drawn individually in `Axes3D.draw()`. I think the root cause is that the coordinate dtypes are not preserved when we build the `pandas.MultiIndex` in `PandasMultiIndex.stack`. We should cast the input variables to their proper dtypes before we build the index, or construct the `MultiIndex` levels explicitly with the desired dtypes. I think we can resolve this by updating `pylint/pyreverse/inspector.py` to check for `astroid.AnnAssign` parents during variable visits. When `visit_assignname` or `handle_assignattr_type` is called, we check if `node.parent` is an instance of `astroid.AnnAssign`. I think the root cause is that pylint's `unused-import` checker is not checking the attribute name of the type annotation when it is an `Attribute` node. In `_store_type_annotation_node` within `pylint/checkers/variables.py`, we should handle `astroid.Attribute` by storing `type_annotation.attrname` to `self._type_annotation_names` so that the imported name is registered as used.

I think we should update `pylint/config/__init__.py` to use `appdirs.user_data_dir('pylint')` for `PYLINT_HOME` when `PYLINTHOME` is not set in the environment. The user report correctly points out that pylint stores data in `.pylint.d` and this data storage should comply with the XDG Base Directory Specification, specifically placing it in the user's data directory (which defaults to `$HOME/.local/share/pylint`). We should import `appdirs` and replace the default fallback path `os.path.join(USER_HOME, '.pylint.d')` with `appdirs.user_data_dir('pylint')`.

I think the root cause is that `SimilarChecker` continues to process modules and report similarities even when `min-similarity-lines` is set to 0. We should update `SimilarChecker.close` to check if `self.min_lines == 0` and return early if so, which will prevent it from running the similarity computation and reporting `R0801` messages when disabled.

I think the root cause of the issue is that the `verbose` option in `pylint/lint/base_options.py` is configured with `_DoNothingAction`, which argparse interprets as requiring an argument because it doesn't specify `nargs`. We should update the `verbose` option definition in `pylint/lint/base_options.py` to use `action="store_true"` instead of `_DoNothingAction`. This will ensure that argparse treats both `--verbose` and `-v` as boolean flags that do not expect any arguments, and it will also fix the help message which currently suggests a `VERBOSE` value is expected. We do not need to modify the preprocessing logic in `pylint/config/utils.py` as this is an argparse configuration issue.

I think the root cause is that in recursive mode, the file paths returned by `_discover_files` start with a `./` prefix (e.g., `./.a/foo.py`). Since `_is_in_ignore_list_re` uses `re.match` which is anchored at the start of the string, it fails to match patterns like `.a` against `./.a/foo.py`. We should update `expand_modules` to normalize the file paths using `os.path.normpath` before checking them against the ignore list and ignore patterns.

I think the root cause is the integer division in the `cpu.shares` path of `_query_cpu` in `pylint/lint/run.py` returning 0 when shares are low. We should update line 60 to `avail_cpu = int(cpu_shares / 1024) or 1` to ensure it defaults to 1.

I think the root cause is that `_is_ignored_file` in `pylint/lint/expand_modules.py` receives relative paths (like `src/gen\about.py` on Windows) which can have inconsistent slash directions when running recursively. We should convert the `element` path to an absolute path using `os.path.abspath(element)` at the beginning of `_is_ignored_file` before matching it against the regex patterns to ensure consistency.

I think the root cause is that `modify_sys_path` assumes the first entry is always the working directory and pops it unconditionally. However, when run from `runpy`, the first entry might be a user-defined path. We should check if `sys.path[0]` is a relative path (like `""` or `"."`) before removing it, as Python only inserts relative paths by default for the current directory when run as a module.

I think the root cause is that pylint's CSV parser `_splitstrip` in `pylint/utils/utils.py` doesn't support escaping commas. Since commas are commonly used in regular expressions (such as quantifiers like `{1,3}`), we should modify `_splitstrip` to allow escaping commas with a backslash (`\,`). This will allow users to write `bad-name-rgxs = "(foo{1\,3})"` in their configuration so that the comma is not treated as a separator, resolving the mangling issue.

I think the issue is that `caplog.clear()` resets `self.handler.records` by assigning a new empty list to it in `reset()`, but the stashed records in `self._item.stash[caplog_records_key]` still point to the old list. To fix this, we should update `LogCaptureFixture.clear()` to also clear the lists inside `self._item.stash[caplog_records_key]` so that `get_records()` returns empty lists after `clear()` is called.

I think the root cause is that `_is_skipped(self.obj)` in `TestCaseFunction.runtest` only checks the test method itself, but doesn't check if the parent class is skipped. Since `self.obj` is the method, it returns `False` when the skip decorator is on the class. We should update the check to see if either the method or its class is skipped by using `_is_skipped(self.obj) or _is_skipped(self.obj.__class__)`.

I think the root cause is that `store_mark` in `src/_pytest/mark/structures.py` does not merge markers from base classes when a subclass is decorated. We should update `store_mark` to check if the target object is a class, and if so, retrieve `pytestmark` from all classes in its `__mro__` and merge them before appending the new mark.

I think the root cause of the TypeError is that _pytest.capture.EncodedFile.write is too strict in Python 3 and does not support writing bytes directly. Since the underlying stream is opened in binary mode, EncodedFile should allow passing bytes through. We should update EncodedFile.write in src/_pytest/capture.py to check if obj is an instance of bytes (or six.binary_type) and write it directly to the buffer instead of raising a TypeError.

I think the root cause is that `p.new` can be a numpy array, and the comparison `p.new in sentinels` raises a `ValueError` because numpy arrays return an array of booleans for equality comparison. We should update `num_mock_patch_args` in `src/_pytest/compat.py` to check if `p.new` is an instance of `numpy.ndarray` before performing the `in` check, and skip it if it is, since a numpy array cannot be a mock sentinel anyway.

I think the root cause is that the serialization logic in `src/_pytest/reports.py` is designed to only serialize a single `reprtraceback` from `longrepr`. Instead of modifying the serialization format, we should update `ExceptionChainRepr` in `src/_pytest/_code/code.py` to compile all the traceback entries from the chain into its `reprtraceback` attribute during initialization. This way, all entries will be automatically serialized and deserialized without changes to `reports.py`.

I think the root cause of the HTTP 400 errors is that `bpaste.net` has deprecated the `python3` lexer value. We should update `create_new_paste` in `src/_pytest/pastebin.py` to use `lexer: "python"` instead of `python3` when running on Python 3, as the `python` lexer is standard and backward-compatible.

I think the root cause is that we are using the lowercased path (returned by `unique_path`) to perform the actual import in `_importconftest`. We should only use `unique_path` to generate a key for `_conftestpath2mod` to avoid loading duplicate conftests on case-insensitive systems, but we must use the original, case-preserved `conftestpath` when calling `pypkgpath()` and `pyimport()` to avoid Windows import folder casing issues.

I think the root cause of the regression is that `Package.collect()` eagerly calls `self._mount_obj_if_needed()`, which attempts to import the package's `__init__.py` file. If this file contains errors or is platform-specific, collection fails. Since these `__init__.py` files are often not test modules themselves, we should wrap the `self._mount_obj_if_needed()` call in `Package.collect()` in a try-except block to catch `ImportError` and `AssertionError`. We can check if the path matches `python_files` patterns, and if it doesn't, we can safely ignore the import failure and proceed with collecting the subdirectories and files.

I think the root cause of the `.[` replacement bug is that `getmodpath()` by default stops at the module level (`stopatmodule=True`), which results in a relative path that can easily be misformatted when parametrized tests are used. If we change the default value of `stopatmodule` to `False` in `getmodpath()`'s definition inside `src/_pytest/python.py`, it will return the complete module path, which prevents this collision. Then we can safely remove the `s.replace(".[", "[")` line because the full path doesn't require this workaround.

I think the root cause of the BytesWarning is that we are trying to format a bytes object directly into a string in `_show_fixture_action`. We should check if `fixturedef.cached_param` is an instance of `bytes` and decode it to a string using `utf-8` before writing it to the terminal writer. This will cleanly format the bytes without triggering any warnings.

I think the root cause is that we don't check if the TestCase class is marked as skipped before postponing `tearDown` in `TestCaseFunction.runtest`. We should update `runtest` to check if `self.parent.obj` has `__unittest_skip__` set to `True`, and if so, skip the `tearDown` postponement.

I think the root cause of the interpreter crash on debug builds is that we are compiling `True`, `False`, and `None` as `ast.Name` nodes with `ast.Load()`. In Python 3.8+, these are reserved keywords and must be represented as `ast.NameConstant` in the AST. We should update `not_expr` in `src/_pytest/mark/expression.py` to detect these specific identifier values and return `ast.NameConstant(True)`, `ast.NameConstant(False)`, or `ast.NameConstant(None)` respectively, which will allow the AST to compile successfully.

I think the root cause is that `evaluate_skip_marks` in `src/_pytest/skipping.py` does not respect the `--runxfail` option. When `--runxfail` is active, we should bypass skip marks as well to ensure all tests are executed. We should add a check `if item.config.option.runxfail: return None` at the beginning of `evaluate_skip_marks`.

I think the root cause is that `evaluate_xfail_marks` in `src/_pytest/skipping.py` relies on `item.iter_markers(name="xfail")`, which only picks up markers defined statically on the test function. When we dynamically add a marker using `request.node.add_marker(mark)`, it is added to `item.keywords` but might not be visible to `iter_markers` during the test run lifecycle. We should update `evaluate_xfail_marks` to check `item.keywords` for the 'xfail' key to correctly identify dynamically added markers.

I think the root cause is that `EncodedFile` (which wraps the temporary file for FD capture) is initialized without specifying the `newline` parameter. By default, `io.TextIOWrapper` uses `None` for `newline`, which enables universal newline translation and converts `\r` to `\n` on read. To fix this and preserve carriage returns, we should initialize `EncodedFile` with `newline='\r'` in `src/_pytest/capture.py`.

I think the root cause is that the `LogCaptureFixture` does not restore the handler's log level during teardown. Since the default log level for pytest logging is `WARNING`, we should update `LogCaptureFixture._finalize` to reset `self.handler.level` to `logging.WARNING` to ensure it is restored for subsequent tests.

I think the root cause is that the `pytest_ignore_collect` hook check in the `_recurse` method of both `Session` (in `src/_pytest/main.py`) and `Package` (in `src/_pytest/python.py`) is incorrectly discarding symlinked directories. We should update `_recurse` to check if the entry is a symlink using `direntry.is_symlink()` and bypass the `pytest_ignore_collect` hook in that case to ensure we don't skip them during collection.

I think the root cause is that `pytest --fixtures` doesn't filter out dynamically generated internal autouse fixtures. Renaming these fixtures in `src/_pytest/unittest.py` might break compatibility with plugins or internal tools that look up these fixtures by their exact names. Instead, we should update the display logic in `src/_pytest/python.py`. Specifically, in `_showfixtures_main`, we can skip any fixture that is marked as `autouse=True` when not in verbose mode. We should update the check to `if verbose <= 0 and (argname[0] == '_' or fixturedef.autouse):` to ensure they are hidden from the normal fixtures list.

I think we should add `store_cv_values=False` to the `RidgeClassifierCV` constructor signature to fix the `TypeError`. Since `RidgeClassifierCV` inherits from `_BaseRidgeCV` and `_BaseRidgeCV` already has `store_cv_values` attribute set up, we just need to expose the parameter in `RidgeClassifierCV`'s `__init__` and we do not need to modify the `super` call.

I think the root cause of the RuntimeWarning and the resulting 'nan' is that `tk` is computed as an integer, which can lead to unexpected behavior during division by the float result of `np.sqrt`. We should cast `tk` to float before the final division in `fowlkes_mallows_score` to ensure proper float division: `return float(tk) / np.sqrt(pk * qk) if tk != 0. else 0.`.

I think the root cause is that `get_feature_names` unnecessarily calls `_check_vocabulary()`, which raises a `NotFittedError` if the vectorizer hasn't been explicitly fitted. Since we just want to retrieve the feature names, we should remove the `self._check_vocabulary()` call from `get_feature_names` in `sklearn/feature_extraction/text.py`. If the vectorizer is not fitted and no vocabulary was provided, it will naturally raise an `AttributeError` when trying to access `self.vocabulary_`, which is standard Python behavior.

I think we should store the refit time in the `cv_results_` dictionary under the key `'refit_time'` instead of exposing it as a new attribute `refit_time_` on the search class. Storing it in `cv_results_` is more consistent with how we handle other timing benchmarks like `mean_fit_time` and `mean_score_time`. We can record the time taken for the final fit when `self.refit` is enabled, and add this value to the `results` dictionary before it is stored in `self.cv_results_`.

I think the root cause is that LogisticRegressionCV inherits from LogisticRegression but its __init__ method does not call super(LogisticRegressionCV, self).__init__(). Because of this, the base class parameters are not initialized correctly, which causes issues when parent methods like predict_proba are called during scoring. We should update LogisticRegressionCV.__init__ to call super and pass the parameters including multi_class.

I think the root cause of the error is that `clone` expects instances of estimators, but receives a class type when a parameter is set to an estimator class. We should update the beginning of the `clone` function in `sklearn/base.py` to check if the `estimator` is a class (type), and if so, instantiate it with default parameters before cloning. This will ensure that `get_params` can be called successfully and we get a valid clone of the estimator.

I think the convergence warning in `plot_sparse_coding.py` is actually caused by a math error in `ricker_function` where `np.pi ** 1 / 4` is used instead of `np.pi ** 0.25`, leading to incorrectly scaled wavelets. If we fix this formula in `examples/decomposition/plot_sparse_coding.py`, the default `max_iter=1000` in `Lasso` is more than enough to converge, so we don't need to modify the `SparseCoder` API to expose `max_iter`.

I think the root cause of the inconsistent `copy_X` behavior in `LassoLarsIC` is that `LinearModel._preprocess_data` is called with `self.copy_X` instead of the `copy_X` parameter passed to `fit`. In `LassoLarsIC.fit`, we have a `copy_X` parameter which defaults to `True`, but then we pass `self.copy_X` to `_preprocess_data` while passing `copy_X` to `lars_path`. We should update the `_preprocess_data` call to use `copy_X` to ensure consistency throughout the `fit` method.

I think the root cause is that we are instantiating a new `KFold` object for each class inside the loop in `_make_test_folds`. This can be inefficient and might lead to inconsistent state. We should instantiate a single `KFold` object outside the list comprehension and reuse it for all classes like this:

```python
        klf = KFold(self.n_splits, shuffle=self.shuffle, random_state=self.random_state)
        per_cls_cvs = [
            klf.split(np.zeros(max(count, self.n_splits)))
            for count in y_counts]
```
This ensures we use a single consistent splitter configuration across all stratification classes.

I think the root cause of the `ValueError: bins must be monotonically increasing or decreasing` is that the `bin_edges` computed in `KBinsDiscretizer.fit` are not sorted when using `strategy='kmeans'`. This happens because `KMeans` does not guarantee that the returned `cluster_centers_` are in the same order as the initialization. To fix this, we should sort the `bin_edges` array for each feature after it is constructed in the `fit` method, before we store it in `self.bin_edges_`. Specifically, we can call `bin_edges[jj].sort()` after merging with `col_min` and `col_max` in `sklearn/preprocessing/_discretization.py`.

I think the discrepancy between `predict` and `fit_predict` when `n_init > 1` is because `fit_predict` performs a final `_e_step` at the very end of the method, which uses the parameters of the last initialization instead of the best one. However, performing this extra `_e_step` is actually redundant. During the EM loop, we already compute `log_resp` for each iteration. We should simply cache the `log_resp` corresponding to the best initialization (inside the `if lower_bound > max_lower_bound:` block) as `best_log_resp` and return `best_log_resp.argmax(axis=1)` at the end of the method. This fixes the discrepancy and also optimizes the method by avoiding an extra E-step on the entire dataset.

I think the traceback indicates that the `-` operator is being used on a boolean array, which is no longer supported in numpy. We should modify `sklearn/linear_model/huber.py` in the `_huber_loss_and_gradient` function to use the `~` operator or `np.logical_not` on `axis0_safe_slice(X, ~outliers_mask, n_non_outliers)` instead of negating it with `-` when `X` has a boolean dtype.

I think we should update the indexing and slicing logic in `__getitem__` in `sklearn/pipeline.py` to handle slice bounds without requiring `len(self)`. Implementing `__len__` on the `Pipeline` class itself is risky because many data validation utilities across scikit-learn, such as `_num_samples` in `sklearn/utils/validation.py`, check for `__len__` to determine sample size. If `Pipeline` implements `__len__`, it might be incorrectly treated as a sequence of samples rather than an estimator by these utility functions, leading to silent bugs. We should instead resolve the slice indices in `__getitem__` using `len(self.steps)` when slice stop or start indices are not specified or are negative.

I think since `IsolationForest` inherits from `BaseBagging`, the `warm_start` parameter and its logic are already fully implemented in the parent class. To expose this functionality, we only need to add `warm_start=False` to the `IsolationForest.__init__` signature and document it. The parent class's `_fit` method will automatically pick up the parameter and handle the incremental tree addition, so we do not need to modify the `super().__init__` call or manually assign `self.warm_start`.

I think the root cause of the AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'fit' is that the utility function has_fit_parameter in sklearn/utils/validation.py does not check if the passed estimator is None before attempting to access its fit method. We should update has_fit_parameter to return False if estimator is None. This will safely handle None estimators when checking for parameter support.

I think the root cause is that `tree_.feature` contains negative values like `_tree.TREE_UNDEFINED` (-2) for leaf nodes, which causes indexing errors when we have fewer features than the absolute value of these undefined markers. We should clean up `tree_.feature` at the start of `export_text` by replacing all `_tree.TREE_UNDEFINED` values with `0` (e.g., using `tree_.feature[tree_.feature == _tree.TREE_UNDEFINED] = 0`) so that we only deal with valid feature indices throughout the export process.

I think the root cause of the IndexError is that self.multi_class is used instead of the resolved multi_class variable when deciding how to average the coefficients in sklearn/linear_model/logistic.py. When self.multi_class is set to 'auto', it incorrectly falls back to the multinomial case's indexing (which expects a 4D array), whereas coefs_paths actually has 3 dimensions because the resolved multi_class is 'ovr'. We should change `self.multi_class == 'ovr'` to `multi_class == 'ovr'` at line 2173 in sklearn/linear_model/logistic.py to fix this indexing error.

I think we should resolve this by updating `ISSUE_TEMPLATE.md` instead of modifying `sklearn/utils/_show_versions.py`. The issue description mentions we can add it to the issue template when sklearn version is > 0.20. This is a cleaner approach because `joblib` is an external dependency that is not strictly required for all scikit-learn installations, so we shouldn't force it into the core `show_versions` output. We should update the template instructions to run `import joblib; print(joblib.__version__)` alongside `sklearn.show_versions()` for users reporting issues with versions > 0.20.

I think the TypeError is caused by NearestNeighbors not accepting float values for n_neighbors in compute_optics_graph. We should fix this by converting min_samples to an integer after scaling it in compute_optics_graph before we instantiate NearestNeighbors. The clustering part in cluster_optics_xi shouldn't be affected since it doesn't use NearestNeighbors.

I think the root cause is that `cross_val_predict` incorrectly attempts to access `estimator.classes_` when dealing with multi-output classifiers that return list predictions. Since `MultiOutputClassifier` does not have a `classes_` attribute, but its individual estimators do, we should update `sklearn/model_selection/_validation.py` to access `estimator.estimators_[i_label].classes_` instead of `estimator.classes_[i_label]` when processing list predictions.

I think the root cause is that `y_small_train` is not decoded before being passed to the scorer in `_check_early_stopping_scorer`. Since we are using a classifier with string targets, the scorer expects strings but receives integers. We should decode `y_small_train` using `self.classes_` in `_check_early_stopping_scorer` before calling the scorer.

I think the root cause of the ZeroDivisionError is that when there are no support vectors, `dual_coef_indices.size` is 0, which makes the step size in `np.arange` 0. We should update the step size calculation in `sklearn/svm/base.py`'s `_sparse_fit` to use `max(1, dual_coef_indices.size) / n_class` instead of `dual_coef_indices.size / n_class` to ensure we always have a non-zero step size.

I think the root cause is that _RepeatedSplits does not inherit from BaseCrossValidator, which is why RepeatedKFold and RepeatedStratifiedKFold do not have the standard __repr__ method. We should update _RepeatedSplits to inherit from BaseCrossValidator in sklearn/model_selection/_split.py to resolve this.

I think the root cause is that we are using NFKD normalization in `strip_accents_unicode`, which decomposes characters and can lead to unexpected behavior if the input is already in NFKD form. We should switch to using NFC normalization instead to ensure consistency, as `unicodedata.combining` expects standard NFC normalized characters.

I think the root cause is that `_wrap_data_with_container` in `sklearn/utils/_set_output.py` does not preserve the original dtypes when creating the pandas DataFrame. Since the data is converted to a numpy array during validation, we lose the original dtypes (like `category` or `float16`). We should update `_wrap_in_pandas_container` to accept a `dtypes` argument, and in `_wrap_data_with_container` we should pass `original_input.dtypes` to it. Inside `_wrap_in_pandas_container`, we can then cast the output DataFrame back using `astype` with these dtypes. This is much simpler than modifying `_validate_data` to avoid ndarray casting.

I think we should add the `fill_value` parameter to `IterativeImputer` to support decision tree-based estimators. Since these estimators (like `HistGradientBoostingRegressor`) can handle missing values natively, we should pass `fill_value` to the estimator's `fit` method in `_impute_one_feature` (e.g., `estimator.fit(X_train, y_train, fill_value=self.fill_value)`) to guide their splitting decisions, rather than passing it to the initial `SimpleImputer` which is only used for the starting values.

I think the root cause of the ValueError is that `_wrap_in_pandas_container` in `sklearn/utils/_set_output.py` directly assigns the original input index to the output DataFrame using `data_to_wrap.index = index`. When a transformer performs aggregation (like grouping), the output DataFrame naturally has fewer rows than the original input, leading to a length mismatch. To fix this, we should use `data_to_wrap = data_to_wrap.reindex(index)` instead of direct assignment to safely conform the output DataFrame to the original input index structure without throwing an error.

I think the warning is raised because `score_samples` calls `_validate_data` with `reset=False` during the `fit` process. Since `fit` is not yet complete when we estimate the offset, we should allow the feature names to be reset during this internal call. We should update `score_samples` to accept a `reset` parameter, defaulting to `False`, and call it with `reset=True` inside `fit` when computing the offset.

I think the root cause is that `cross_val_score` in `sklearn/model_selection/_validation.py` does not support generator inputs for the `cv` parameter because it gets consumed during validation. We should update `cross_val_score` to convert `cv` to a list if it is a generator or iterator before passing it to `cross_validate`.

I think we should update `roc_curve` in `sklearn/metrics/_ranking.py` to check if the maximum threshold is less than or equal to 1, and if so, clip the thresholds to not exceed 1. We can implement this at the end of the function before returning:

```python
    if thresholds.max() <= 1:
        thresholds = np.clip(thresholds, None, 1)
```
This will ensure that we don't return thresholds greater than 1 when dealing with probability estimates.

I think the root cause is that `ColumnTransformer._hstack` does not properly handle mixed output formats when the `remainder` parameter is an estimator. While the main transformers have their output configured to pandas, the `remainder` estimator returns a NumPy array. This mismatch causes `_hstack` to fallback to `np.hstack` and lose all DataFrame structure and dtypes. I think we should update `_hstack` in `sklearn/compose/_column_transformer.py` to check if `transform='pandas'` is configured, and if so, dynamically wrap the NumPy array output of the remainder estimator into a pandas DataFrame before concatenating them with `pd.concat`.

I think the discrepancy between n_jobs=1 and n_jobs > 1 arises because the sequential loop in `k_means` modifies the shared `random_state` object in-place across iterations, whereas the parallel execution path uses independent seeds. To ensure that sequential runs don't suffer from state mutation side-effects, we should update the sequential loop to pass a copy of the `random_state` (or re-initialize it using the initial seed) at each iteration, preventing the state from carrying over between runs.

I think the issue is that `dedent_filter` is executed after `prepend_filter` and `append_filter` in the filters list. Since it runs last, any prepended or appended text also gets dedented, which strips their leading whitespace and causes warnings. To fix this, we should update the `prepend_filter` and `append_filter` methods in `sphinx/directives/code.py` to check the `dedent` option. If `dedent` is specified, we should pad the prepended/appended strings with the same amount of spaces before adding them, so that they end up with the correct indentation after the `dedent_filter` slices them.

I think the root cause is that Pygments LaTeX formatter wraps the inline code in a `Verbatim` environment by default, which introduces extra newlines that translate to space characters in the PDF. We should use Pygments' built-in `nowrap=True` option for the formatter when highlighting inline code in `visit_literal`. This will prevent Pygments from wrapping the output in `Verbatim` and avoid the spacing issue altogether. We should pass `nowrap=True` to the `self.highlighter.highlight_block` call in `visit_literal` in `sphinx/writers/latex.py`.

I think the root cause is that `merge_typehints` in `sphinx/ext/autodoc/typehints.py` is processing classes, which leads to adding the return type of `__init__` (which is `None`) to the class documentation. Since classes themselves don't have return types in the same way functions do, we should avoid merging type hints for classes entirely. I suggest adding a check at the beginning of `merge_typehints` to return early if `objtype == 'class'`.

I think the root cause is that the `Message` class in `sphinx/builders/gettext.py` does not filter out duplicate locations when it is initialized. The `locations` list is passed directly from the catalog metadata, which accumulates all occurrences of a message, including duplicates from the same file and line. We should update the `__init__` method of the `Message` class to deduplicate the `locations` list using `self.locations = list(set(locations))`. This will resolve the duplication in the output POT files while keeping the code simple and localized to the message data structure. We might also need to check if similar changes are needed in `babel.messages.catalog.Message` if we use it in some configurations.

I think the root cause is that `html_visit_inheritance_diagram` in `sphinx/ext/inheritance_diagram.py` is hardcoded to prepend a single `../` to URLs when `graphviz_output_format` is `SVG`. This doesn't work for nested documents because they are deeper in the directory structure. We should calculate the nesting depth of the current document using `self.builder.current_docname` and prepend the appropriate number of `../` relative to the document depth to ensure the links in the SVG point to the correct location.

I think we can resolve this by treating 'genindex', 'modindex', and 'search' as special virtual documents in the toctree. We should update `sphinx/directives/other.py` to bypass the nonexisting document check for these specific names and add them to the entries.
