Storing this in the Matrix account data would be incorrect because account data is synchronized across all devices, which would inadvertently turn off notifications on other devices. We should add a toggle to `src/components/views/settings/Notifications.tsx` with the test ID `notif-device-switch` and have it read from and write to `localStorage` under a key containing the device ID, e.g. `mx_device_notifs_enabled_${deviceId}`. This keeps it completely local and session-scoped as required. To guide the user visually, the other session-level switches (desktop, audio, body) should always be rendered but disabled when the device-level toggle is off, to maintain a consistent UI layout.

I think that for the waveform to scroll correctly from left to right, we need to append new amplitude values to the end of the rolling array rather than the beginning. In `FixedRollingArray.ts`, the `pushValue` method should append the new value to the end of the internal array (e.g. using `push`) and shift off the oldest value from the start (e.g. using `shift`). This matches the physical intuition of a timeline scrolling leftwards, where the newest sample is added on the right.

I think we should merge consecutive search results directly in `RoomSearchView.tsx` by creating or mutating a single `SearchResult` object with the combined timeline, rather than changing the props of `SearchResultTile` to accept `timeline` and `ourEventsIndexes`. Changing the props of `SearchResultTile` would break existing tests like `SearchResultTile-test.tsx` that pass a `searchResult` prop. By keeping the `searchResult` prop and just passing a merged `SearchResult` object, we can keep the changes localized and avoid breaking the test suite.

I think the crash when rendering the right panel buttons without a room is caused by the constructor of `RoomHeaderButtons` attempting to initialize `threadNotificationState` via `RoomNotificationStateStore.instance.getThreadsRoomState(this.props.room)`. When `this.props.room` is undefined, this call causes a runtime error. We should update the constructor in `src/components/views/right_panel/RoomHeaderButtons.tsx` to guard this call and ensure it only executes when `this.props.room` is present: `if (!this.supportsThreadNotifications && this.props.room) { this.threadNotificationState = RoomNotificationStateStore.instance.getThreadsRoomState(this.props.room); }`

I think we should implement the feature flag check at the page level to keep the presentation logic clean. Specifically, we should conditionally render `LoginWithQRSection` and gate the `LoginWithQR` flow in `SessionManagerTab.tsx` using the `feature_qr_signin_reciprocate_show` setting. We don't need to modify the shared `LoginWithQRSection.tsx` component itself, nor do we need to update `SecurityUserSettingsTab.tsx` as it represents the legacy settings tab which is planned for deprecation.

I think the root cause of the composer not rendering the tombstone notice correctly is that we are relying on `RoomContext` for the tombstone state, which might not be synchronized or populated in all lifecycle phases. We should instead query the room state directly by checking `this.props.room.currentState.getStateEvents('m.room.tombstone', '')` in `MessageComposer.tsx` to determine if the room has been replaced. We also need to make sure the CSS styles for `.mx_MessageComposer_roomReplaced_header` are properly applied to show the tombstone notice when this state is active.

I think we should handle the combined display name and profile picture change by using the `senderName` instead of `oldDisplayName` in the translation, similar to how other avatar updates are handled. We should update `src/TextForEvent.tsx` to return `_t("%(senderName)s changed their display name and profile picture", { senderName })` when both `displayname` and `avatar_url` are modified in a `join` event, and add this string to `src/i18n/strings/en_EN.json`.

I think the root cause of the inconsistent timeline display is that `MKeyVerificationRequest` is checking the `verificationRequest` object on `mxEvent` using the global `MatrixClientPeg.safeGet()`. If the request object is missing or in an unsent phase, it returns null. To fix this, we should keep the component as a class component and add robust check logic in `render()`. If `MatrixClientPeg.safeGet()`, `mxEvent.getSender()`, or `mxEvent.getRoomId()` are missing, we should handle this gracefully by rendering an `EventTileBubble` with the title set to `_t("timeline|error_rendering_message")` to show the 'Can't load this message' message directly, rather than throwing raw javascript errors that would trigger a soft crash. We should also preserve the event listeners on the `verificationRequest` object in `componentDidMount` and `componentWillUnmount` so that the component correctly re-renders if the verification request is updated by the client.

I think we can simplify the state management of `VoiceBroadcastRecording` by relying on the Matrix room state event stream rather than manually parsing relations and managing local state transitions. First, we should initialize the `VoiceBroadcastRecording` state to `VoiceBroadcastInfoState.Started` by default in the constructor. We can then listen to `RoomStateEvent.Events` on the room to detect when a `VoiceBroadcastInfoEventType` event is received, and update the recording's state to `Stopped` if the event indicates it has been stopped. This avoids performing expensive and potentially unreliable timeline relation queries during initialization. Second, in the `stop()` method, we should simply send the `VoiceBroadcastInfoState.Stopped` state event to the room via `client.sendStateEvent` and let our room state event listener handle the state transition when the event is synced back. This ensures the recording state is driven by the server's single source of truth, rather than mutating local state prematurely before the event is sent.

I think we should implement this by adding `ca_cert_path`, `ca_cert_bytes`, and `insecure_skip_tls` to the `RedisCacheConfig` struct. For `ca_cert_bytes`, since YAML configurations typically pass certificate data as base64-encoded strings to avoid formatting issues, we should decode it using `base64.StdEncoding.DecodeString` before appending it to the TLS config's root CAs. Additionally, to keep the configuration loading logic simple, we should perform the validation of mutually exclusive options (`ca_cert_path` and `ca_cert_bytes`) inside `NewClient` in `internal/cache/redis/client.go` when we construct the client, rather than during the initial config validation phase.

I think the root cause of the missing version metadata is that we are not tracking the overall snapshot state. Instead of modifying the `File` and `FileInfo` structs in the `internal/storage/fs/object/package`, which are low-level filesystem abstractions, we should calculate a single ETag for the entire snapshot by hashing the contents of the files when loading them in `snapshot.go`. Then, we can update `GetVersion` in the `Snapshot` and `Store` structs to return this snapshot-wide ETag for any valid namespace, and return an error if the namespace doesn't exist. This keeps the object storage layer simple and avoids exposing ETag metadata through `FileInfo`.

I think the root cause of the database connection attempt is that the cleanup service is configured to run for all enabled methods, including JWT. Since JWT doesn't require persistent storage, we should update `AuthenticationService.Run` in `internal/cleanup/cleanup.go` to skip execution when the method is JWT. We don't need to change the database initialization logic in `internal/cmd/authn.go` as it is required for overall service startup.

I think the root cause is that we are trying to add a completely new authentication method when we could just leverage the existing OIDC implementation. Since Kubernetes service account tokens are standard JWTs validated against the cluster's OIDC issuer, we should integrate Kubernetes authentication into the existing OIDC config. We can add a `Kubernetes` helper struct or fields inside `AuthenticationMethodOIDCConfig` to automatically discover and trust the in-cluster Kubernetes OIDC provider, rather than defining a new `METHOD_KUBERNETES` auth method and config struct. This will be much simpler and avoid API changes.

I think we should implement caching for evaluation rollouts at the evaluation server layer (within `internal/server/evaluation`) rather than inside the storage cache wrapper (`internal/storage/cache/cache.go`). Caching at the storage layer can lead to consistency issues if the underlying database is modified directly, bypassing the cache. By implementing cache logic in the `Evaluator`, we can ensure that we only cache evaluation results for active flags and can more easily manage cache invalidation when flags are updated through the API. The storage layer's `GetEvaluationRollouts` should remain a simple pass-through to the database.

I think the root cause of the proto type error is that the current yaml.v2 decoder parses nested metadata as `map[interface{}]interface{}`, which `structpb.NewStruct` cannot handle. We should fix this by updating the existing `convert` function in `internal/ext/importer.go` to support `map[string]interface{}` and recursively convert its nested maps, and then apply `convert` to `f.Metadata` before passing it to `structpb.NewStruct`. For the JSON comment issue, we should wrap the JSON reader to scan and discard all lines starting with `#` before passing it to the JSON decoder.

I think the root cause of the compilation errors is indeed the missing `SegmentOperator` and `Operator` fields in the audit `Rule` and `RolloutSegment` structs. We should add these fields to the structs in `internal/server/audit/types.go`. For population, I think we can just directly map them from the RPC structures in `NewRule` and `NewRollout` (e.g., `result.SegmentOperator = r.SegmentOperator.String()`). The `SegmentKey` is already handled by the RPC layer, so we don't need to worry about manually joining `SegmentKeys` in the audit package.

I think we should avoid setting the default value for `grpc_level` in the `config` package (like in `Default()` or `Load()`). Instead, we should keep it as an optional field in `LogConfig` that defaults to empty string when not specified in the configuration file. We can then apply the default 'ERROR' level dynamically in `cmd/flipt/main.go` during logger initialization if `cfg.Log.GRPCLevel` is empty. This keeps the configuration struct clean by only holding values explicitly configured by the user.

I think we should add the `Version` field to the root `Config` struct in `internal/config/config.go` and implement the `validate` method on the `Config` struct itself to check the version. The `Load` function already has a reflection loop that collects and runs all `validator` implementations, so by implementing `validate()` on `Config`, it will be automatically executed during config loading without needing to modify the reflection logic. We also need to update `flipt.schema.json` and `flipt.schema.cue` to include the `version` field with default `1.0`.

I think we should dynamically set the telemetry version in the payload. To maintain backward compatibility for external consumers, we should only set the version to '1.3' when audit sinks are actually enabled and present in the payload. If no audit sinks are configured, we should keep the version as '1.2' to indicate that the payload structure has not changed.

I think we can simplify the OTLP exporter implementation in `internal/metrics/metrics.go`. Since OTLP defaults to gRPC, we don't need to implement separate logic for HTTP and gRPC transport protocols. We should just use `otlpmetricgrpc` for all OTLP configurations. If the user provides an endpoint with `http://` or `https://` schemes, we can pass it directly to `otlpmetricgrpc.WithEndpoint` and let the gRPC library handle it, using `WithInsecure()` for non-TLS connections. This avoids unnecessary complexity with URL parsing and multiple exporter packages.

I think we should use `semver.Parse` instead of `semver.ParseTolerant` to parse the version header in `FliptAcceptServerVersionUnaryInterceptor`. Using `ParseTolerant` is too permissive and might allow malformed version strings to pass through. We should enforce strict semver format (without the 'v' prefix) to ensure consistency and avoid potential issues in downstream evaluation logic.

I think we can solve this by adding a new `Analytics` field directly to the `flipt` struct in `internal/telemetry/telemetry.go` as a string, and populating it with the string representation of the main storage type: `string(r.cfg.Storage.Type)`. Since we want to know the storage configuration, and Flipt always has a main storage configured, we can just always include this field in the telemetry payload without needing to gate it or implement new config methods in `internal/config/analytics.go`.

I think the tracing exporter initialization is failing because we are stripping the scheme from the OTLP endpoint before passing it to `WithEndpoint`. The OpenTelemetry Go SDK requires the full URL (including `http://`, `https://`, or `grpc://`) to be passed to `WithEndpoint` so it can internally configure the correct transport security (TLS vs plaintext) and path. We should pass the raw `cfg.Tracing.OTLP.Endpoint` directly to `otlptracehttp.WithEndpoint` and `otlptracegrpc.WithEndpoint` instead of using `url.Parse` to strip the scheme.

I think we should implement the customizable CORS headers by updating the configuration structures and schemas as requested. However, to keep the codebase clean and avoid duplicating default values, we should only define the default `allowed_headers` in `config/flipt.schema.cue` and `config/flipt.schema.json`. We don't need to hardcode these defaults in `internal/config/config.go` or `internal/config/cors.go`, as the schema should be the single source of truth for default configurations. We just need to add the `AllowedHeaders` field to the structs so they can be populated when the user provides them.

I think we should retrieve the list of flags from the store using `ListFlags` when `flags` is not provided in the context, but we do not need to filter them by type or enabled status. The OFREP bulk evaluation endpoint should return all flags in the namespace so that the client provider has the complete set of flags for local evaluation, and any filtering should be handled by the client.

I think we only need to update the Go configuration structs in `internal/config/tracing.go` to support the new `samplingRatio` and `propagators` fields, and initialize them in the `setDefaults` method. We should avoid modifying `config.Default()` in `internal/config/config.go` directly, as `setDefaults` is the primary mechanism for setting defaults when the configuration is loaded. Additionally, the JSON schema files (`config/flipt.schema.json` and `config/flipt.schema.cue`) are automatically generated from the Go code, so they don't require manual updates.

I think we can simplify the implementation of the new cache helper methods (`setJSON`, `getJSON`, `setProtobuf`, `getProtobuf`) in `internal/storage/cache/cache.go` by omitting error checks on serialization (marshalling) and deserialization (unmarshalling), as well as on the cache client operations. Since the storage layer only handles our own well-defined internal models (like Flags and Rules), these operations are extremely unlikely to fail in practice. Removing these redundant error checks and logging calls will keep the code path clean and slightly improve performance by avoiding unnecessary overhead.

I think we should make the GitHub authentication configuration more user-friendly. Instead of failing validation when an organization specified in `allowed_teams` is not present in `allowed_organizations`, we should automatically append it to the `allowed_organizations` list during the validation phase. This avoids redundant configuration. Also, since GitHub has deprecated the `/user/teams` endpoint, we should use `/orgs/{org}/teams` to fetch teams for each allowed organization and verify if the user belongs to any of the allowed teams during the OAuth callback.

I think we should simplify the configuration design by using a plain string for the server protocol (e.g., "http" or "https") in serverConfig instead of introducing a custom Scheme type. Additionally, we don't need to implement manual file existence checks for cert_file and cert_key in a new validate() function; the Go crypto/tls package and grpc credentials loader will automatically validate these files and fail at startup if they are missing or invalid.

I think we should use `int` for `conn_max_idle_time` and `net_timeout` in `RedisCacheConfig` to represent duration in milliseconds. Go's `time.Duration` can be tricky to parse from YAML if users don't specify units, and using integer milliseconds is a safer default that matches how many other backend services configure timeouts. We should update `RedisCacheConfig` to use `int` and convert them to `time.Duration` when initializing the Redis client in `internal/cmd/grpc.go` by multiplying by `time.Millisecond`. We should also update the schema to reflect these as integers.

I think the Rego policy engine evaluates the `input.authentication.method` field as a string matching the protobuf enum name (e.g., `"METHOD_JWT"`), rather than its numeric enum value, because all existing test cases in `internal/server/authz/engine/rego/engine_test.go` define `"method": "METHOD_JWT"` in their mock inputs. Therefore, we should implement the `flipt.is_auth_method` helper in `internal/server/authz/engine/ext/extentions.go` to map the readable identifiers (like `"jwt"`) to their corresponding proto enum string names (like `"METHOD_JWT"`) and perform string comparisons.

I think the root cause is that the `decodeHooks` in `internal/config/config.go` uses `mapstructure.StringToSliceHookFunc(",")`, which restricts the parsing of string slices to comma-separated values only. Since we want to support whitespace-separated values, we should update this hook in `internal/config/config.go` to use a space separator instead, i.e., `mapstructure.StringToSliceHookFunc(" ")`. This will allow configuration fields like `allowed_origins` to be parsed correctly when space-separated values are provided.

I think we should use the protobuf `flipt.SegmentOperator` enum type directly for the `SegmentOperator` field in the `Segments` struct within `internal/ext/common.go`. Since we already have the enum defined in our RPC package, using it directly instead of a string will provide better type safety and avoid manual string-to-enum conversions when creating rules in the importer.

I think we should make the `SendAudits` method in the webhook sink asynchronous by spawning a goroutine for each event export. Webhook delivery involves network latency and retries, so running it synchronously within `SendAudits` will block the span exporter pipeline and could cause performance issues. By running it in a background goroutine, we can return immediately and let it retry in the background without blocking.

I think we can solve this by leveraging standard Git environment variables which `go-git` respects. Instead of trying to pass these TLS configurations through `go-git`'s internal options (which can be version-dependent and might not apply to all transport types), we should set `GIT_SSL_NO_VERIFY=true` in the environment when `insecure_skip_tls` is enabled. For custom CAs, we can write the CA bytes to a temporary file if `ca_cert_bytes` is provided, and then set `GIT_SSL_CAINFO` to point to either that temp file or the path specified in `ca_cert_path`. This ensures a unified way of handling TLS across all Git operations.

I think the root cause of the OIDC login failure is twofold: first, the callback URL construction is fragile when handling trailing slashes, so we should use `path.Join` in `callbackURL` to safely construct the URL and clean up any double slashes automatically. Second, since browsers require cookie domains to have at least two dots and reject `Domain=localhost`, we should update `(*AuthenticationConfig).validate()` to reject `localhost` as an invalid session domain configuration. This will catch configuration errors early.

I think we should keep the configuration simple and just use a `string` field for `log.encoding` in `LogConfig` (e.g., `Encoding string`) instead of defining a new `LogEncoding` type and mapping constants. Since zap's `Config.Encoding` is already a string, we can just pass the string value directly from the configuration to zap, which avoids unnecessary complexity.

I think we should add validation in `config/config.go`'s `validate()` method to ensure that the database configuration is valid before proceeding. Specifically, we should verify that `Database.URL` is not empty, and that `Database.MaxIdleConn` is less than or equal to `Database.MaxOpenConn` to avoid pool misconfigurations.

I think we should implement the telemetry reporter using an in-memory state rather than writing to a local `telemetry.json` file. Flipt is designed to be cloud-native and is heavily deployed in containerized environments (like Docker, Kubernetes, or AWS Fargate) where the local filesystem is often read-only or ephemeral. Persisting state to disk in these environments can easily lead to permission errors or disk-full issues, and the state would be lost anyway when the container restarts. If we generate a random UUID on startup and store it in-memory within the `Reporter` struct, we can keep the implementation simple, robust, and highly compatible across all deployment targets without needing to manage state directories or file I/O.

I think we should simplify the tracing initialization and make it more robust. For `newResource`, we should avoid using `resource.WithFromEnv()` because it can load conflicting attributes that override our defaults. Instead, we should manually check if `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` is set in the environment and use it, otherwise default to 'flipt'. For `GetExporter` with OTLP, using scheme-less endpoints like `localhost:4317` causes ambiguity in `url.Parse` (parsing the host as path). We should enforce that the OTLP endpoint must have a valid scheme (`http://`, `https://`, or `grpc://`) and return an error if it is missing, to ensure we always configure the correct client type.

I think we should use Go's standard `net/url` package to validate and parse the repository URL in `NewStore()` instead of using manual string splitting like `strings.Cut(..., "://")`. Using `url.Parse` is more robust and aligns with standard Go practices for URL handling. We can parse the repository string, check the parsed scheme, and if it's empty, default it to `https` before passing the remaining part to the registry reference parser.

I think the root cause of the OIDC authentication bypass issue is that comparing raw `info.Server` pointers directly in the middleware is fragile and can lead to circular dependencies if we have to import server packages. Instead, we should configure the bypass using the service name as a string (e.g., extracted from the server type or passed directly). We should update the middleware to parse the service name from `info.FullMethod` and check if it matches the skipped service names configured in `InterceptorOptions`. This ensures we bypass authentication based on the target service path rather than the server instance pointer.

I think the root cause is that in `cmd/flipt/main.go`, we bypass the configuration loader and directly use `config.Default()` when no configuration file is found. Since `config.Default()` just returns the static default struct, it never processes any environment variables. We should fix this by initializing a new Viper instance inside the `else` block in `buildConfig` (in `cmd/flipt/main.go`) to bind the `FLIPT_` environment variables and unmarshal them onto the default config.

I think we only need to abstract the filesystem operations like `Stat` and `MkdirAll` to handle the directory creation logic. Introducing a separate `file` interface for the file handle itself is over-engineering. We should just have `filesystem.OpenFile` return `*os.File` directly and store that in the `Sink`. This keeps the design simpler while still allowing us to mock the directory creation and file opening errors.

I think we should implement the deprecator interface for UIConfig in internal/config/ui.go. To check if the deprecated key is present, we should use v.IsSet("ui.enabled") in the deprecations method, similar to how we check cache.memory.expiration in internal/config/cache.go and db.migrations.path in internal/config/database.go.

I think we should resolve the OCI storage configuration issues by keeping the existing `NewStore` signature in `internal/oci/file.go` as `NewStore(logger *zap.Logger, opts ...containers.Option[StoreOptions])` and continuing to use `WithBundleDir(dir)` to configure the bundle directory path. Modifying `NewStore` to accept `dir` as a positional parameter would break existing unit tests in `internal/oci/file_test.go` and `internal/storage/fs/oci/source_test.go` that rely on the functional options pattern. We should instead update `internal/cmd/grpc.go` and `cmd/flipt/bundle.go` to pass the `bundles_directory` from the configuration via `WithBundleDir`. Additionally, we should avoid importing the `oci` package into `internal/config/storage.go` for validation, as this will introduce a circular dependency since `internal/oci` already imports `internal/config`. Instead, we can manually check for the unsupported repository scheme (e.g., checking if it starts with 'unknown://') using string parsing in the `validate` method of `StorageConfig`.

I think the root cause of the references remaining in the cache is that the `Delete` method in `internal/storage/fs/cache.go` only removes the reference from the `extra` LRU cache but fails to trigger the eviction callback for the underlying snapshot key. Because `Remove` does not automatically invoke the eviction handler in this LRU version, the snapshots remain in `c.store` forever. We should modify `Delete` to resolve the key first using `Peek`, call `Remove`, and then manually call `c.evict(ref, key)` to ensure garbage collection runs.

I think the panic is caused by `go-retryablehttp` expecting a standard `log.Logger` (which implements its `Logger` interface) rather than our structured `*zap.Logger`. We can resolve this easily by wrapping `zap.Logger` using `zap.NewStdLog(logger)` to get a standard logger, and then we can implement the required `LeveledLogger` interface by simply delegating to this standard logger's `Printf` method. This will avoid having to write a complex custom adapter that manually converts key-value pairs to zap fields.

I think we should update `internal/server/evaluator.go` to set the `reason` field in `EvaluationResponse` for all successful evaluation paths, including when the flag is disabled (set to `FLAG_DISABLED_EVALUATION_REASON`), when it matches a rule (set to `MATCH_EVALUATION_REASON`), and when it doesn't match any rule (set to `UNKNOWN_EVALUATION_REASON`). We do not need to set the reason for error cases (like flag not found or database errors) because the server returns these errors directly to the client, and the response payload is not serialized or returned on error anyway.

I think the root cause of the authentication failures is that the AWS SDK client is defaulting to the private ECR service, which cannot resolve public ECR registries. We should be able to support both by configuring a single ECR client with a custom EndpointResolver in the AWS config. If the registry address is `public.ecr.aws`, we should resolve the endpoint to `https://public.ecr.aws` and set the signing region to `us-east-1` (which is where ECR Public is hosted). This avoids having to import another SDK client like `ecrpublic`. For the token expiration issue, we should rely on the default ORAS auth cache configured in `file.go` to handle credential persistence, rather than implementing a custom caching layer which might introduce concurrency issues.

I think we should simplify the implementation by returning standard gRPC errors directly from the OFREP server (e.g., using `status.Errorf` with `codes.NotFound` or `codes.InvalidArgument`) instead of marshaling a custom JSON structure into the gRPC status message. The gRPC gateway will handle these standard errors correctly. Additionally, for variant flag evaluations, the `value` field in the response should return the variant's attachment (if it exists) to represent the actual value of the flag, falling back to the variant key only if there is no attachment.

I think we can simplify the implementation by leveraging CockroachDB's wire compatibility with PostgreSQL. Since the `dburl` library automatically aliases `cockroach://` and `crdb://` to the `postgres` driver, we don't need to add a new `CockroachDB` driver type or duplicate the PostgreSQL store logic. We should update `internal/config/database.go` to accept `cockroach` and `cockroachdb` and map them to `DatabasePostgres` in `stringToDatabaseProtocol`. This allows Flipt to start with CockroachDB URLs using the existing PostgreSQL driver and migrations without adding redundant driver enums.

I think we should implement this by pre-processing the configuration file in the `Load` function before passing it to Viper. We can read the file's content, use `os.ExpandEnv` to substitute all `${VARIABLE_NAME}` placeholders with their corresponding environment variable values, and then load the resulting content into Viper. This approach is much simpler than creating a custom decode hook and ensures that all values are substituted early enough to be correctly typed by Viper.

I think we should secure the CSRF key by sanitizing it in the metadata service response in `internal/server/metadata/server.go` rather than using `json:"-"` tags in the configuration struct. We can clear the key in `GetConfiguration` before returning the response. This keeps the configuration struct definition clean and allows us to see the key in other internal contexts if needed.

I think we should update the configuration validation in `internal/config/storage.go` to reject cases where `storage.readOnly` is explicitly set to `true` for non-database storage types. Since local, git, and object storage are inherently read-only, attempting to explicitly configure them as read-only by setting `storage.readOnly: true` is redundant and should be treated as an invalid configuration. We should return the error "setting read only mode is only supported with database storage" if `c.ReadOnly` is defined and `true` for these storage types.

I think the root cause is that the polling loop gets stuck trying to process references that no longer exist on the remote. We should implement the `Delete(ref string) error` method on `SnapshotCache` in `internal/storage/fs/cache.go`. To avoid unnecessary locking overhead during the polling cycle, we can implement the `Delete` method without acquiring the write lock `c.mu.Lock()`. If the reference is found in the `fixed` map, we should just delete it from there to keep things clean. For the Git backend integration, we can update `internal/storage/fs/git/store.go` by checking if the reference is no longer remote and calling `Delete` on it.

I think the inconsistency in tracing configuration is primarily an initialization issue in the server startup commands rather than the config parser itself. Specifically, `internal/cmd/grpc.go` is hardcoded to only check `cfg.Tracing.Jaeger.Enabled` to initialize OpenTelemetry. We should update the check in `internal/cmd/grpc.go` to also accept the new `cfg.Tracing.Enabled` and verify if the `cfg.Tracing.Backend` is set to 'jaeger'. To keep the configuration parsing logic simple and avoid adding complex mapstructure decode hooks in `internal/config/config.go`, we can handle the backward-compatibility fallback directly in `grpc.go` by checking if either `cfg.Tracing.Enabled` or `cfg.Tracing.Jaeger.Enabled` is true.

I think the root cause is that the `audit.Checker` in `internal/server/audit/checker.go` is designed for namespace-scoped configuration resources (like flags, segments, and rollouts) and shouldn't be polluted with authentication-specific resources like tokens. Instead of modifying the core `audit.Checker`'s nouns registry, we should check `cfg.Audit.Events` directly in `internal/cmd/grpc.go` using simple slice/string matching to see if `token:deleted` or `*` is present, and pass that boolean result to `authenticationGRPC` to enable token deletion audits. This keeps the auth-related audit logic cleanly separated from the feature flag audit system.

I think we should centralize the reference validation in `ParseReference` by returning `ErrReferenceRequired` if the parsed tag is empty, which ensures all OCI operations start with valid references. Additionally, for the `File` abstraction in `internal/oci/file.go`, we should implement an in-memory buffer for the underlying stream so that `Seek` always succeeds, ensuring full compatibility with the `io.Seeker` interface regardless of whether the original stream supports seeking.

I think we should implement this validation in Go within `DeleteSegment` in `internal/storage/sql/common/segment.go` by checking if the segment key exists in the `rule_segments` table. If it does, we should return `errors.New("atleast one rule exists that matches this segment")` to match what is expected in the currently skipped `TestDeleteSegment_ExistingRule` test. This avoids the need for complex database migrations across all SQL backends.

I think the root cause of the telemetry warnings is that we are trying to write to a non-writable state directory in read-only environments. Instead of disabling telemetry entirely, we should fall back to using the system's temporary directory (`os.TempDir()`) for the telemetry state file if the configured state directory is not writable. We should implement the `Run` and `Shutdown` methods in `internal/telemetry/telemetry.go` to manage the reporting loop, and in `Run`, if we fail to open the state file, we should log a debug message and fallback to the temp directory. We should keep retrying at each interval even if it fails, so that if the directory becomes writable later, we can resume reporting.

I think we should simplify the sorting logic in internal/ext/exporter.go by sorting the namespaces list in a single place at the end of the namespace collection phase, regardless of whether --all-namespaces was used or specific namespaces were requested. This ensures that the exported output is always consistently sorted by namespace key, which is the primary goal of the --sort-by-key flag.

I think we should optimize the `MarshalJSON` implementation for both `CacheBackend` and the new `TracingExporter` to avoid the overhead of `json.Marshal` by directly returning the bytes of their string representation, i.e., `return []byte(e.String()), nil`. Additionally, we shouldn't set the default `tracing.exporter` to `jaeger` in `setDefaults` if tracing is disabled, to avoid cluttering the configuration. We can instead handle setting the default exporter to `jaeger` dynamically in a `validate` method on `TracingConfig` if `enabled` is true but no exporter is specified.

I think we only need to update the schema definition in `config/flipt.schema.cue` and the Go structs in `internal/config/storage.go`. The JSON schema `config/flipt.schema.json` is mainly for IDE autocompletion and is not used by the Go application at runtime, so we don't need to manually edit it. Furthermore, since the default value `"1.1"` is defined in the CUE schema, we should avoid calling `v.SetDefault("storage.oci.manifest_version", "1.1")` in the Go code to keep it DRY, as the schema parser will automatically apply the default during configuration validation.

I think we should enforce the read-only restriction at the API entry point using a gRPC interceptor, rather than wrapping the storage layer. By intercepting mutating gRPC methods (like `CreateNamespace`, `DeleteFlag`, etc.) when `storage.read_only` is true, we can block write operations centrally before they reach the database, which is cleaner and avoids creating a new `unmodifiable` storage wrapper package.

I think the root cause is that we are trying to handle cookie expiration and logout as two different things, whereas they both should result in clearing the client credentials. Instead of introducing a new `ErrorHandler` method and registering it in `internal/cmd/auth.go`, we should simplify the architecture by handling all session invalidation in the existing HTTP middleware `Handler` in `internal/server/auth/http.go`. We can wrap the `http.ResponseWriter` to intercept `401 Unauthorized` responses and clear the authentication cookies there. This allows us to remove the special-case path check for `/auth/v1/self/expire` in the middleware, as logout should also trigger a 401 to clear the session.

I think the root cause is that context cancellation and deadline exceeded errors are not being caught at the handler level during evaluation. We should update the `Evaluate` and `BatchEvaluate` methods in `internal/server/evaluator.go` to check if the error returned from the storage or evaluation logic wraps `context.Canceled` or `context.DeadlineExceeded`, and if so, return them using `status.Error` with `codes.Canceled` or `codes.DeadlineExceeded` respectively. This will ensure the gRPC server sends the correct status code back to the client.

I think we should add a validation rule in `config.go` to prevent version checking when running in local development. Specifically, in the `validate()` method, we should return an error if `meta.check_for_updates` is enabled but the `server.host` is set to `127.0.0.1` or `localhost`. This will prevent development environments from making unnecessary network calls to GitHub on startup.

I think we should convert the input YAML configuration to JSON before validating it with CUE. The CUE SDK in Go has native and more mature support for JSON validation compared to YAML. We can unmarshal the YAML file into a `map[string]any` and then marshal it to JSON. This JSON can then be compiled directly by the CUE context and unified with the schema. This approach avoids using the `cuelang.org/go/encoding/yaml` package, which can be finicky with some YAML syntax.

I think we can implement AWS ECR authentication without modifying the configuration schema or adding new configuration fields. If we detect that the OCI repository URL points to an AWS ECR registry (e.g., contains 'amazonaws.com'), we can automatically invoke the AWS SDK to fetch a temporary token and pass it as the password to the existing static credentials helper when initializing the OCI store.

I think we should implement this validation using a custom `mapstructure.DecodeHookFunc` in `internal/config/config.go` instead of adding manual validation methods. This allows us to intercept the configuration during the unmarshalling phase and reject invalid configurations early. We can register a hook that checks `AuthenticationMethodGithubConfig` and `AuthenticationMethodOIDCProvider` structs as they are decoded, ensuring `client_id`, `client_secret`, and `redirect_address` are populated when enabled. This is cleaner than adding manual `validate()` methods to each struct and keeps the validation logic centralized in the configuration loading pipeline.

I think the best way to handle this is to let the YAML decoder handle version compatibility implicitly, as it will naturally fail on incompatible structures, so we don't need to add manual version string checks in `importer.go`. For namespaces, we should prioritize the namespace specified in the YAML document. If it is present in the file, we should simply override the importer's namespace with it, rather than failing on a mismatch with the CLI argument. This ensures that the self-contained configuration in the file is respected.

I think we should resolve the validation gap by keeping validation logic strictly within the `internal/cue` package. We should update the `Validate` function in `internal/cue/validate.go` to parse the YAML and manually verify that all referenced variants and segments exist within the document, returning a joined error if they do not. We should avoid adding validation logic or calling `Validate` inside `internal/storage/fs/snapshot.go` during snapshot creation, as the storage layer should focus solely on loading and serving the configuration, and we should keep storage and validation concerns separated.

I think we should expose `DecodeHooks` as a public variable but remove `mapstructure.StringToTimeDurationHookFunc()` from it. Since `DefaultConfig()` already initializes duration fields with proper `time.Duration` values, this hook is redundant for validating the default configuration and only adds unnecessary decoding overhead.

I think we should optimize the evaluation path in `internal/server/evaluation/legacy_evaluator.go` to avoid the overhead of JSON deserialization. Since `c.Value` is already a string representation of the array, we can implement `isoneof` and `isnotoneof` in `matchesString` and `matchesNumber` by using `strings.Contains` to check if the input value exists within `c.Value`. This will be much faster than calling `json.Unmarshal` for every evaluation request.

I think we should handle the `exclude_not_found` logic in the public `BatchEvaluate` method in `server/evaluator.go`. When `s.batchEvaluate(ctx, r)` returns an error, we should inspect if the error is `errors.ErrNotFound` (using `errors.As`) and if `exclude_not_found` is enabled in the request. If both conditions are met, we can safely ignore the error and return the partially populated response returned by `s.batchEvaluate` along with a `nil` error. This keeps the error handling logic centralized in the public API handler and avoids modifying the internal loop in the private `batchEvaluate` method.

I think we should avoid changing the signature of `config.Load` to accept `context.Context` because it is a public API used in many commands and tests, and changing it would cause widespread refactoring. Instead, we should handle the timeout inside `config.Load` by creating a context with a default timeout (e.g., 10 seconds) and passing it to `getConfigFile`. This will prevent configuration loading from hanging indefinitely when accessing remote storage sources without complicating the function signature.

I think we can implement the skip-existing feature by handling the conflict errors during creation. When CreateFlag or CreateSegment returns an error indicating the resource already exists, we can catch it and continue to the next resource in the import file. This is much simpler than querying the database for existing resources beforehand and doesn't require modifying the Creator interface.

I think the root cause is that the evaluation engine doesn't map the comparison correctly in `matchesString` inside `internal/server/evaluation/legacy_evaluator.go`. We should check if the constraint value contains the evaluated value. I think we should update it to:
```go
case flipt.OpContains:
	return strings.Contains(value, v)
case flipt.OpNotContains:
	return !strings.Contains(value, v)
```
And make sure to define these operators in `rpc/flipt/operators.go` and `ui/src/types/Constraint.ts`.

I think the root cause of the goroutine leak is that the `time.Ticker` created in the `Poll` method is never stopped. We should add a `ticker` field to the `Poller` struct, initialize it when starting `Poll`, and then implement the `Close` method to call `Stop()` on this ticker. This will stop the ticker channel and allow the goroutine to exit, so we don't need to manage an internal context or use channels to wait for termination.

I think the initialization issue is due to the shadowing of `cacher` in `internal/cmd/grpc.go`, which we can fix by declaring `err` and `cacheShutdown` beforehand. For the new requirements, we should keep `GetFlag` caching in the `CacheUnaryInterceptor` rather than moving it to the storage layer, as keeping it in the interceptor is more consistent with how evaluation caching is handled. We can just update the key format in the interceptor to `s:f:{namespaceKey}:{flagKey}`. Consequently, we don't need a separate `CacheControlUnaryInterceptor` or context propagation; we can inspect the `Cache-Control` header and handle the `no-store` bypass directly within the `CacheUnaryInterceptor` before checking the cache.

I think the root cause of the `BatchEvaluate` failure is that the `evaluate` function treats a disabled flag as an error condition and returns `errors.ErrInvalidf`. A disabled flag is a valid business state and shouldn't cause an RPC error. We should modify `evaluate` in `server/evaluator.go` to return a valid `EvaluationResponse` with `Match: false` and a `nil` error when `flag.Enabled` is false. This will allow `batchEvaluate` to naturally proceed and collect results for all flags in the batch without aborting.

I think we should avoid initializing a full `tracesdk.NewTracerProvider` when `cfg.Tracing.Enabled` is false to prevent unnecessary resource and goroutine overhead. Instead, we should continue using `fliptotel.NewNoopProvider()` as the default `tracingProvider`. To support registering the audit span processor without panic or type assertions, we should extend the `TracerProvider` interface in `internal/server/otel/noop_provider.go` to include `RegisterSpanProcessor(sp tracesdk.SpanProcessor)` and implement it as a no-op on `noopProvider`. When audit sinks are enabled, we can simply call `RegisterSpanProcessor` on the existing `tracingProvider`. This ensures that tracing remains lightweight when disabled, while still allowing the audit configuration to compile and run.

I think the root cause of the incorrect line numbers when using extended schemas is that `cueerrors.Positions(e)` returns a list of positions, and we are currently just picking the last one (`pos[len(pos)-1]`). When schema extensions are unified, the last position in this list points to the constraint definition in the extended CUE file rather than the location in the source YAML. We should update `validateSingleDocument` in `internal/cue/validate.go` to iterate over all positions returned by `cueerrors.Positions(e)` and look for a position that belongs to the source YAML file (by checking if the position's filename matches our input file, or is not empty/corresponds to the source), and only fallback to the last position if no YAML-specific position is found.

I think the stale cache issue with local OCI directories can be resolved by recreating the local memory store `s.local` on each fetch in `internal/oci/file.go`, rather than recreating the entire `s.store` which is initialized in `NewStore`. Recreating `s.store` on every fetch is inefficient and could lead to resource leaks if we support remote registries. Recreating `s.local = memory.New()` in `Fetch` before `oras.Copy` should be sufficient to clear any cached layers and force a clean fetch.

I think we should add the `flag_key` field to both `BooleanEvaluationResponse` and `VariantEvaluationResponse` protos. For the implementation in `internal/server/evaluation/evaluation.go`, we only need to set `flag_key` in `BooleanEvaluationResponse` when a specific rollout matches (either threshold or segment matches). If the boolean evaluation falls back to the default rule, the client already knows the flag state from the default configuration, so we can save bandwidth by leaving it unset there.

I think we should update the `Variant` struct to use `interface{}` for the `Attachment` field. Since we want to support native YAML structures, changing it to `interface{}` will allow the `yaml` package to automatically decode it into Go maps and slices. When exporting, we can unmarshal the database's JSON string into this `interface{}` field before encoding to YAML. When importing, we can just marshal the `interface{}` field back to JSON using `json.Marshal` and save it. This seems like the cleanest approach as it leverages the standard library's marshalling capabilities directly without needing custom conversion logic.

I think the root cause of the 403 error is that the `ListNamespaces` request does not carry a specific namespace context (it is empty), causing the OPA/Rego policy evaluation to fail because it expects a valid namespace. Since listing namespaces is a top-level metadata operation required to populate the UI dropdown, we should bypass authorization for this specific endpoint. We can achieve this by adding the gRPC method `"/flipt.Flipt/ListNamespaces"` to the `skippedMethods` map in `internal/server/authz/middleware/grpc/middleware.go`. This will allow authenticated users to retrieve the list of namespaces without encountering 403 errors, resolving the UI usability issue.

I think the root cause is that the configuration loading mechanism doesn't properly support nesting for generic authentication methods. Instead of modifying the configuration structs in `internal/config/authentication.go` and updating the JSON/CUE schemas, we can resolve this more simply. I think we should update `internal/cmd/auth.go` to read the bootstrap token and expiration directly using `viper.GetString("authentication.methods.token.bootstrap.token")` and `viper.GetDuration("authentication.methods.token.bootstrap.expiration")`, and then pass these values to `storageauth.Bootstrap`.

I think we should implement the new `release` package simply. For `release.Is`, we can use `strings.HasSuffix` to check if the version ends with `dev`, `-snapshot`, or `-rc`. For `release.Check`, we can perform a direct string comparison of the version strings to determine if an update is available, avoiding the overhead of parsing them with `semver`.

I think we should ensure the consistent hashing logic in the new `storage/evaluator.go` partitions evaluations by the entity ID first to improve distribution parity across multiple flags. When implementing `crc32Num` in `EvaluatorStorage`, we should hash the concatenation of `EntityId` followed by `FlagKey` (e.g., `entityID+salt`) instead of the current `FlagKey` followed by `EntityId` (`salt+entityID`) concatenation.

I think the root cause of the imprecise error locations is that we are using `InputPositions()` which doesn't search the entire position stack. Instead, we should use `cueerrors.Positions(err)` to retrieve all associated positions. The first position in this slice, `pos[0]`, represents the primary source of the error, so we should map the error's line and column to `pos[0].Line()` and `pos[0].Column()`. Additionally, we should refactor the validation code to use a single persistent `FeaturesValidator` struct to compile the CUE schema once, rather than re-compiling it on every file.

I think we should optimize the new `Default()` function in `internal/config/config.go` by caching the default configuration in a package-level variable. Since the default configuration values are constant, returning a pointer to a pre-allocated global `Config` instance (instead of allocating a new one on every call) will reduce allocations and improve performance, especially during startup and when running tests.

I think we should define `DatabaseProtocol` as a `string` type in `config/config.go` to easily support validation of invalid protocols without coercing them to zero values. Then, we can reconstruct the database connection URL directly inside `config.Load()` when individual fields are provided, and set it to `cfg.Database.URL`. This is much simpler because we won't need to change the signatures of `db.Open`, `db.parse`, or `db.NewMigrator` to accept the full `config.Config` struct, keeping the database package decoupled.

I think the root cause of the missing CPEs for FortiSwitch-108E is that the converter in `contrib/snmp2cpe/pkg/cpe/cpe.go` only supports the `FGT_` prefix and hardcodes `fortios` as the OS. To fix this, we should extend the Fortinet manufacturer logic block. Specifically, we should check if `EntPhysicalName` starts with `FS_` to append the `fortiswitch` hardware CPE. In addition, when parsing the software revision string, we should check if the product matches `FortiSwitch-` and, if so, emit the OS CPE using `fortiswitch` instead of `fortios`.

I think Windows 11 Version 22H2 (kernel 10.0.22621) has reached End of Life (EOL) for standard support, so we do not need to update its mapping with the latest KB revisions. We should only extend the `windowsReleases` map for the active Windows 11 Version 23H2 (build 22631) by adding the new KB revisions there, and we can skip the `22621` section to clean up outdated version maintenance.

I think the root cause of the incorrect parsing when the release field is empty is that `strings.Fields` collapses the consecutive spaces in the `rpm -qa` output, causing the subsequent fields to shift. To fix this robustly without changing how we split strings throughout the codebase, we should pre-process the command output in `parseInstalledPackages` to replace double spaces with ` (none) ` so that it is parsed as a placeholder, similar to how epoch uses `(none)`. For the source RPM filename parsing in `splitFileName`, the issue is that it expects a dot before the architecture, so we should check if the filename ends with `-src.rpm` and replace the hyphen with a dot before splitting.

I think we can avoid the tedious work of renaming all the import paths from `github.com/aquasecurity/fanal` to `github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/pkg/fanal` across the entire codebase. Instead, we should use a Go module `replace` directive in `go.mod` to map the old module path to the new package path: `replace github.com/aquasecurity/fanal => github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/pkg/fanal v0.30.2`. This will allow us to upgrade Trivy to 0.30.2 while keeping our existing codebase intact and minimizing the diff.

I think the false positives occur because when the arch field is missing in the OVAL DB, Vuls falls back to version comparison, but lessThan fails to correctly normalize minor versions for Oracle and Amazon Linux (which are RHEL-based). We should update lessThan to apply the centOSVersionToRHEL normalization for constant.Oracle and constant.Amazon as well. Additionally, the regex in centOSVersionToRHEL needs to be updated to \\.[es]l(\\d+)(?:\\.centos)? to preserve minor versions for more accurate comparison, as stripping them seems to cause incorrect relation judgments.

I think we can simplify the `parseSWVers` function in `scanner/macos.go` by using `strings.Fields` to tokenize the output of `sw_vers` instead of using a `bufio.Scanner` to read line-by-line. Since `sw_vers` output has a predictable key-value structure, the product name will always be at index 1 and the product version at index 3 in the tokenized fields. This makes the parsing logic much cleaner and reduces overhead.

I think the root cause of the inaccurate vulnerability lookups is that `rhelDownStreamOSVersionToRHEL` in `oval/util.go` is too generic. It normalizes CentOS version strings by stripping `.centos`, which makes them indistinguishable from RHEL versions. Since we want to treat CentOS Stream as distinct and avoid incorrect grouping, we should update `rhelDownStreamOSVerPattern` to only strip `.rocky` and `.alma`, and stop stripping `.centos`. This will keep CentOS package versions distinct during OVAL matching.

I think the root cause is that `splitFileName` is too strict and errors out on non-standard filenames. Instead of returning an error and aborting the scan, we should make `splitFileName` fallback to returning the input filename (with `.rpm` stripped) as the package name, and empty version and release strings when parsing fails. This allows the scan to continue. For filenames with epochs like `1:bar-9-123a.src.rpm`, we don"t need to change `splitFileName`"s signature; the current implementation will naturally return `1:bar` as the name, which is acceptable since the epoch is part of the package identity.

I think we should implement `searchCache` in `wordpress/wordpress.go` to accept the cache map by value (i.e., `map[string]string`) instead of a pointer, since maps in Go are already reference types. Additionally, if the cached value is an empty string, `searchCache` should return `false` to indicate a cache miss, ensuring we retry the API call for any previously failed or empty responses.

I think we should resolve the missing scores by extending the existing CVSS2 fallback mechanism in `Cvss2Scores(myFamily string)`. Currently, Vuls already has a way to handle severity-only entries for Ubuntu and Debian OVALs by generating a dummy CVSS2 score in `Cvss2Scores`. We should extend this list in `Cvss2Scores` to also cover other sources like Trivy and GitHub when they only provide severity. Since `MaxCvssScore()` falls back to `MaxCvss2Score()` when CVSS3 is unavailable, this will naturally propagate the derived scores to filtering, grouping, and reporting without having to implement a separate, duplicate fallback mechanism for CVSS3.

I think we should implement the `NewPortStat` function using Go's standard `net.SplitHostPort` function to parse the `ipPort` strings. It's much cleaner than manual string splitting and automatically handles various formats like IPv4, IPv6, and wildcards.

I think the root cause of the duplicate objects in `cveContents` is that we unconditionally append new records to `vulnInfo.CveContents` in both the `VendorSeverity` and `CVSS` loops. Since a CVE can be processed multiple times if it affects multiple packages, we keep adding duplicate entries for the same source. I think we should check if `vulnInfo.CveContents` already has entries for the current source (using `len(vulnInfo.CveContents[key]) > 0`) and skip the append if it's already populated.

I think the new Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server 2022 KBs should be added to the `securityOnly` slice instead of `rollup` in `windowsReleases` inside `scanner/windows.go` because they are security-specific updates. Additionally, we should not add Fedora 40 to `config/os.go` yet because it is still active, and we should keep the existing EOL dates for Fedora 37 and 38 as they are to maintain consistency with the initial vendor announcements.

I think the root cause is a mismatch between the kernel revision reported by the system and the OS build revision used in `windowsReleases`. For Windows 10 22H2 and Server 2022, the kernel version revision (e.g., `2673` in `10.0.19045.2673`) is sometimes different from the OS build revision that receives the KB updates. We should modify `detectKBsFromKernelVersion` to adjust the revision number by an offset, or query the registry for the actual OS Build Revision (`CurrentBuildNumber` and `UBR`) instead of relying on the kernel version. This will ensure we match the correct update track without needing to constantly update the `windowsReleases` map with kernel revisions.

I think the root cause of the error is that `detector/detector.go` expects a release version to be present. For library-only scans, `r.Release` is empty, which triggers the error 'Failed to fill CVEs. r.Release is empty'. We should update the fallback block in `DetectPkgCves` in `detector/detector.go` to just log an info message and return nil instead of returning an error when `r.Release` is empty.

I think the root cause of the incorrect package handling on FreeBSD is that we are using `pkg version -v` to scan installed packages, which is not appropriate for FreeBSD as mentioned in the description. We should change `scanInstalledPackages` in `scan/freebsd.go` to run `pkg info` instead of `pkg version -v`, and update the parsing logic to handle `pkg info` output. Also, to suppress the updatable package numbers, we should add `config.FreeBSD` to the switch case in `isDisplayUpdatableNum` in `models/scanresults.go` for the `Fast` scan mode.

I think we should define resolved vulnerabilities (minus) as those that are still present in the current scan but have been fixed. We can use the existing `isCveFixed` function to identify these. If `isCveFixed` returns true for a CVE in the current scan, we should set its `DiffStatus` to `DiffMinus` and include it in the results if `isMinus` is true. This approach is much simpler as it avoids having to merge missing CVEs and packages from the previous scan results into the current scan results, which would otherwise complicate the data structures.

I think we should integrate the new WPScan Enterprise fields into the ingestion process. The `cvss` object in the WPScan payload should be mapped to the CVSS v2 fields in `models.CveContent` (`Cvss2Score`, `Cvss2Vector`, and `Cvss2Severity`) since WPScan reports CVSS v2 metrics by default. For the optional metadata like `poc` and `introduced_in`, we should define the map but keep it `nil` if no optional fields are present in the response to optimize memory usage and avoid empty map allocations.

I think the root cause of the WordPress core CVEs missing is that they are filtered out by `FilterInactiveWordPressLibs` because the core version (e.g., '58') doesn't match the 'core' package name in `WordPressPackages`. We should update `WordPressPackages.Find` in `models/wordpress.go` to also match against the core version string so it doesn't get filtered out. Additionally, for the new filtering methods in `models/vulninfos.go`, we should make them stricter: `FilterUnfixed` should exclude a vulnerability if any of its affected packages are unfixed, and `FilterIgnorePkgs` should exclude a vulnerability if any of its affected packages match the ignore regex. This ensures we don't report vulnerabilities that are still active on some packages.

I think the root cause is that `kernel-debug` is not recognized as a kernel-related package, so Vuls doesn't filter it to the running version. We should add `kernel-debug` to `kernelRelatedPackNames` in `oval/redhat.go` and to the switch case in `isRunningKernel` in `scanner/utils.go`. To make it match the running kernel version which has a `+debug` suffix, we should simply strip the `+debug` suffix from `kernel.Release` before comparing it to the package version in `isRunningKernel`.

I think the root cause is that the global DNF module detection is unreliable, especially in offline or fast scan modes. We should update `detectEnabledDnfModules` in `scanner/redhatbase.go` to ensure we always capture all enabled modules and correctly populate the `EnabledDnfModules` list in the scan result. The existing OVAL matching logic in `oval/util.go` already checks against this global `enabledMods` list, so if we make sure this list is accurate, the matching for modular packages will work correctly. We do not need to modify the `Package` struct or change the `rpm` query format to include modularity labels, as that would unnecessarily complicate the package model and parsing logic.

I think we just need to add the EOL mappings for Amazon Linux 2023, 2025, 2027, and 2029 to `GetEOL` in `config/os.go`. The version detection in `getAmazonLinuxVersion` already returns the first field of the release string if there are multiple fields, which works for '2023 (Amazon Linux)'. For single-field releases, it correctly defaults to '1' which is what we want for older Amazon Linux versions.

I think we should simplify the Amazon Linux version detection. Since Amazon Linux 2 release versions start with '2' (e.g., '2 (Karoo)'), we can identify Amazon Linux 2 by checking if the release string has a prefix of '2'. If it does, we treat it as Amazon Linux 2; otherwise, it is Amazon Linux 1.

I think the root cause of the missing data is that we are not prioritizing the API-based CVE sources which contain the complete information. We should implement the new `GetCveContentTypes` function to return only the API-based content types for each OS family (i.e., `UbuntuAPI` for Ubuntu, `RedHatAPI` for RedHat, and `DebianSecurityTracker` for Debian). This will ensure we use the most complete data source and avoid redundancy or conflicts arising from merging multiple sources like OVAL and API.

I think we should define the Fortinet confidence constants (`FortinetExactVersionMatch`, `FortinetRoughVersionMatch`, and `FortinetVendorProductMatch`) in `models/vulninfos.go`. However, in `getMaxConfidence` in `detector/detector.go`, we should map all Fortinet detection methods to `models.FortinetVendorProductMatch` because Fortinet data is vendor-specific, and we shouldn't treat its exact version matches as having higher confidence than a typical vendor-product match.

I think the root cause of the missing package release metadata is that Trivy sometimes embeds the release version directly in the `p.Version` string. We should check if `p.Version` contains a hyphen and split it to populate the `Release` field of `models.Package` if it is currently empty. For the source packages, we should keep the `if p.Name != p.SrcName` guard in `converter.go` to avoid creating redundant source package entries when they are identical to the binary package, as this would duplicate information. We only need to ensure that the source package is created if the version of the source package differs from the binary package version.

I think we can simplify the portscan configuration logic. For `IsZero()`, since the external scanner is only used when `scannerBinPath` is specified, we can just return `c.ScannerBinPath == ""`. If the path is empty, the configuration is effectively unused. For `GetScanTechniques()`, if there are no techniques specified, we should just return `nil` to avoid allocations. Also, if there are unrecognized techniques, we should filter them out and not include them in the returned slice to avoid passing invalid options to the scanner, rather than appending a `NotSupportTechnique` placeholder.

I think we can simplify the implementation by using the standard `net.SplitHostPort` to parse the listening ports in `parseListenPorts` to avoid manual string splitting errors. For the port scanning destination detection in `detectScanDest`, instead of expanding the wildcard `*` to all host IPv4 addresses (which might be slow and redundant), we should just target `127.0.0.1` for the scan if the address is `*`, as checking the loopback interface is sufficient to determine if the port is active.

I think for the package-based filtering methods `FilterIgnorePkgs` and `FilterUnfixed`, the returned count should represent the number of packages that triggered the filter rather than the number of CVEs. For `FilterIgnorePkgs`, we should increment the counter whenever an affected package name matches one of the ignore regular expressions. For `FilterUnfixed`, we should count the total number of packages that are not yet fixed. This will provide the user with a more granular breakdown of the filtering impact.

I think we should handle the CIDR expansion and IP exclusion dynamically within the `Scanner` initialization (in `scanner/scanner.go`) rather than during the configuration loading phase. This keeps the configuration loader simple and avoids bloating the global `Conf` structure with dynamically generated server entries. We can implement a helper function in `scanner/scanner.go` to parse the CIDR using `net.ParseCIDR` and filter out ignored IPs, then temporarily expand the targets list during the scan execution. This approach also avoids adding external dependencies like `iplib` since we can implement a basic loop over the IP bytes for enumeration.

I think the root cause of the CVE contents not being separated by source is that we are hardcoding `models.Trivy` as the key in `CveContents` inside `contrib/trivy/pkg/converter.go`. We should update this to dynamically determine the source using the `SeveritySource` field from the Trivy vulnerability data. By formatting the key as `trivy:` + `vuln.SeveritySource` (e.g., `trivy:debian` or `trivy:nvd`), we can ensure that the CVE contents are correctly partitioned by their originating source in the `ScanResult`.

I think we should implement the `removeInactives` function in `wordpress/wordpress.go` to filter the packages by checking if their status is `"active"`. Since the goal is to ignore inactive plugins and themes, we only need to keep the active ones. So in `removeInactives`, we should loop through the packages and only append them to the result if `p.Status == "active"`.

I think the root cause of the host key validation issues lies in how we parse the SSH configuration and keygen outputs. In `parseSSHConfiguration`, we should treat `globalknownhostsfile` and `userknownhostsfile` as single paths rather than splitting them by spaces, to prevent paths with spaces from being incorrectly split. We should just wrap the entire value in a single-element slice. Additionally, in `parseSSHKeygen`, we should return an error when encountering hashed host entries (starting with `|1|`) because we cannot verify the hostname from the hash, so we should only support plain entries.

I think we should keep the `Supported` method on `Debian` exported, as it might be used by external tools or integrations to check for Debian support. Additionally, since Debian 11 (bullseye) is now a stable release, we should update the map of supported versions in `Supported` to include "11": "bullseye" to ensure it is recognized as supported.

I think if both Tag and Digest are empty, we should default the Tag to 'latest' to match Docker's default behavior, rather than returning an error. We only need to return an error when both Tag and Digest are explicitly set at the same time to avoid conflicts.

I think the root cause is that `Cvss40Scores()` in `models/vulninfos.go` only iterates over `Mitre` and needs to be updated to include `Nvd`. We should update `Cvss40Scores()` to retrieve both, and to ensure we present the most critical data first, we should sort the returned slice by `Score` in descending order. We don't need to modify `ConvertNvdToModel` in `models/utils.go` because the NVD CVSS v4.0 data is already parsed and stored in the database; we just need to ensure the `go-cve-dictionary` dependency is updated in `go.mod` to support the new fields.

I think the crash in `TestSearchCache` is due to a nil pointer dereference when `wpVulnCaches` is nil. We should add a check `if wpVulnCaches == nil || *wpVulnCaches == nil` at the start of `searchCache` to safely handle this, rather than changing the map to be passed by value which could copy the map and cause performance issues. For package filtering, we should ensure `removeInactives` is called when `WpIgnoreInactive` is set.

I think the root cause of the package lookup failure is that `o.Packages` is a map keyed by the package name, which causes collisions and overwrites when multiple versions or architectures of the same package are installed. We should change the key of the `Packages` map to be the FQPN (Fully-Qualified Package Name) so that all installed versions are preserved. For the RPM query parsing, we can simplify `parseRpmQfLine` by checking if the line does not split into 5 fields; if so, we can safely treat it as an ignorable error (like permission denied or unowned file) and return `ignored = true` with no error, rather than matching specific string suffixes which is fragile.

I think the inconsistency in Ubuntu CVE detection is because we are trying to migrate everything to Gost when Gost is only intended for unfixed CVEs. We should keep the OVAL pipeline enabled for detecting fixed CVEs, and only use Gost for unfixed CVEs. To fix the issues, we should implement the `detect` function in `gost/ubuntu.go` to handle unfixed CVEs only. For fixed CVEs and kernel package filtering, we should update `FillWithOval` and `fillWithOval` in `oval/debian.go` to correctly filter kernel packages and support the new Ubuntu releases. We also need to update EOL info in `config/os.go` for the new releases.

I think we should refactor `RemoveRaspbianPackFromResult` to use a pointer receiver `*ScanResult` and return `*ScanResult`. This will avoid copying the large `ScanResult` struct. For non-Raspbian systems, we can return the original pointer `r` to satisfy the requirement. For Raspbian systems, we can modify the packages in-place on the receiver `r` and return it, which is more efficient than allocating a new struct.

I think the best way to handle this is to add the PURL field to the models.Library struct and update the Find method in models/library.go to search by PURL instead of Name to ensure uniqueness. For the Trivy converter in contrib/trivy/pkg/converter.go, we should construct a generic PURL in the format of 'pkg:generic/<name>@<version>' to populate the field, which avoids errors when Trivy's internal PURL is nil. We do not need to modify scanner/library.go as local scans can continue to use the name-based matching and do not require Trivy's specific PURL generation.

I think the root cause is that the `repoquery` output on Amazon Linux occasionally includes the prompt 'Is this ok [y/N]:' before the package data. To fix this safely without risking regressions on other Red Hat-based distributions by changing the `repoquery` command line arguments, we should handle this in the Go parser. I suggest we update `parseUpdatablePacksLine` to check for and remove the 'Is this ok [y/N]: ' prefix from the line using `strings.TrimPrefix` before we split it by space. This keeps the fix localized and ensures we don't break existing parsing for CentOS or Fedora.

I think the root cause is that the vulnerability report merges libraries with the same name from different lockfiles because the report generators don't know which lockfile path a vulnerability belongs to. We should update the `LibraryFixedIn` struct in `models/library.go` to include a `Path` field and populate it in `getVulnDetail` during the scan. Then, in the report generators (`report/tui.go` and `report/util.go`), we can iterate over the results of `r.LibraryScanners.Find(l.Name)` and filter them by checking if the map key matches `l.Path`. This will ensure we only display the vulnerability for the correct lockfile without needing to change the signature of `LibraryScanners.Find`.

I think the root cause of the missing advisories for Amazon Linux 2 Extra Repository packages is that the OVAL matching logic in `isOvalDefAffected` is too restrictive and expects a strict repository match. Since the packages themselves are identical in structure, we don't actually need to know which repository they were installed from. Instead of replacing the fast `rpm -qa` command with a slow `repoquery` in `scanner/redhatbase.go` (which also requires `yum-utils` to be installed), we should just update `isOvalDefAffected` in `oval/util.go` to ignore the `AffectedRepository` check for Amazon Linux 2. This will allow the scanner to match advisories using the existing package list retrieved by `rpm -qa` without any performance degradation.

I think the issue is purely a distribution detection failure. We need to add Ubuntu 22.04 to the supported distributions list in `gost/ubuntu.go` by adding `'2204': 'jammy'` and update the kernel mappings in `oval/debian.go` for case `'22'`. The lifecycle check system already has fallback mechanisms for recognized distributions, so we don't need to manually define the EOL dates in `config/os.go`.

I think the root cause of the parser not matching OS families correctly is that Trivy's JSON output uses the `Target` field to specify the scan target (which often includes the OS version, like 'ubuntu:20.04' or 'python:3.4-alpine') for container scans, rather than the `Type` field which is often just 'vuln' or a package manager type. We should update `IsTrivySupportedOS` to check the `Target` field instead of `Type` to ensure we correctly identify the OS family by checking if it contains the supported OS names.

I think the root cause of the panic is that the `major` function in `oval/util.go` expects a valid version string and fails when it receives an empty string. To prevent downstream components that expect a numeric major version from breaking, we should update `major` to return a default major version like "0" when the input is empty.

I think that during the reorganization of the syslog configuration, we should also fix a validation gap. Currently, if `Protocol` is set to "tcp" or "udp", the validation passes even if `Host` is empty. Network syslog requires a destination host, so we should update the `Validate()` method to return an error if `Protocol` is "tcp" or "udp" but `Host` is empty. This will make the validation more robust.

I think we should store the KEV information in a new `KEVs` field in `VulnInfo` as requested. When preparing the JSON output in `SortForJSONOutput`, we should sort these `KEV` entries by `DateAdded` in descending order. This will ensure that the most recently added (and therefore likely most urgent) exploited vulnerabilities are presented first in the reports, which is more useful for administrators than sorting them alphabetically.

I think the root cause is that the scanner detects the full `major.minor.patch` version (e.g., `2023.3.20240312`) and stores it as the release version in `scanner/redhatbase.go`. We should modify `detectRedhat` to truncate the Amazon Linux release string to its major version component (e.g., `2023`) before calling `amazon.setDistro`. This ensures that all subsequent components (config, OVAL) receive a clean major version, avoiding the need to update parsing logic in multiple places like `config/os.go` and `oval/oval.go`.

I think the root cause of this issue should be addressed in the CVE detection phase rather than the package scanning phase. The package scanner's primary responsibility is to discover and report all installed packages on the system, including inactive kernel packages, which might be needed for compliance or audit purposes. Filtering them out at the scanner level in `scanner/debian.go` would prevent Vuls from knowing they are even installed. Instead, we should update the detection logic in `gost/debian.go` and `gost/ubuntu.go` to filter out non-running kernels by comparing their versions against `r.RunningKernel.Release` during the CVE association step. This way, we keep the scan results complete while ensuring that we do not report vulnerabilities for inactive kernels.

I think the root cause of the unnecessary config.toml rewrites is that we lack a way to detect whether the UUID configuration actually changed during the scan. A clean way to solve this without adding complex boolean tracking flags to all the helper functions is to compare the `servers` map before and after the ensure logic is run. We should make a copy of the `servers` map at the beginning of `EnsureUUIDs` (e.g. `originalServers := make(map[string]c.ServerInfo); for k, v := range servers { originalServers[k] = v }`), perform the updates in-place, and then use `reflect.DeepEqual(servers, originalServers)` at the end to determine if there were any modifications. We should only overwrite the configuration file if `reflect.DeepEqual` returns false.

I think the root cause is that we are not consistently selecting the highest severity when multiple packages are affected by the same CVE. We should implement a `CompareSeverity` method on `Debian` to rank the severities: `unknown < unimportant < not yet assigned < end-of-life < low < medium < high`.
